entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: July 23, 1975 Interview

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: [Interview conducted by Judy Carlson at Bessie Murphy's home.]
bracketed_corrections: [Interview conducted by Judy Carlson at Bessie Murphy's home.]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was born 1894 in Elsie, Oregon and we came here [Benton County] in the Spring of 1900.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Tell us about your family.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My father [Stephen Alexander] came with his family in 1878 from Kansas. My mother [Kate Crees Gragg] came with her father [W. M. Crees] in 1871 from Pennsylvania. They met through my father's sister and my mother being in school together. My mother went out to Clatsop County and taught a year of school. She met my father and the romance started.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was your father a farmer?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. He had a farm which now contains the new high school [Crescent Valley High School] on Highland Way, and it also contains the site of an old Indian camp. He used to dig up broken Indian bowls and arrowheads.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And your grandfather?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My maternal grandfather was William Crees and my paternal grandfather was Henry C. Gragg. They came late enough to come on the train from San Francisco and up the coast by ship. My Gragg grandparents came on the old Ajax ship. My grandfather Crees was a farmer too, on King's Road and Highland Way, off Grant Street. And the old house he built in 1878 is still standing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And the Crees building downtown fThird Street]?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was built on the site of his later home after he retired. His daughter named the building after him.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of farm did he have?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He had general farming and a dairy farm. My father was just general farming [grain raising]. You don't have all your eggs in one basket in those days. Stock, grain, sheep, etc. 200 acre farm Dad had.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What are some of your early memories growing up on the farm? And when did you start school?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: 1901 . . . and I had to walk two miles through people's pastures and woods to get down to what is 9th Street now where the school was (District 45). And one of the pleasures of my childhood was having a pony and riding everywhere. In fact, I rode a pony clear through high school; I started in the town school in 4th grade and I figured it up once, 11,000 miles. The high school I went to was located in Central Park and I graduated in 1914. And on the farm we had -- for those days -- quite a large cherry orchard, and they were old-fashioned varieties like Governor Woods, Oxhart, and Black Republicans. No Royal Annes, or Lamberts or Bings. People would come from as far away as Summit to pick the cherries and can them right there. I had a wonderful time playing with the kids.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you pick the cherries?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, we also picked them to ship them on the train for people west towards the coast. We would pick them early in the morning and with the stems on so they would keep.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember your grandparents?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, Grandpa Crees was a wonderful man, and he just loved to mow hay. After he retired, he came out and mowed hay for my father. And in those days, there were lots of jack

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: rabbits, and sometimes in the mowing he'd scare up a jack rabbit, and always the farm dog was with him . . . and then there'd be a race. And Grandpa would be the fan, and he'd yell, "Sic 'em Shep!"

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And your grandmother?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She died in Pennsylvania. And the other grandparents lived in Clatsop County. After we came. . . well, grandpa died in 1900. Grandpa Crees was very nice. He gave me that little chair. He always had a horse and buggy and I've ridden with him lots of times. He was always happy and singing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think people were happier then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, they didn't have so many worries. And life was simpler. They had high standards and morals, and of course, very set in their ways about it. They wouldn't be as lenient then as we are now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And when they disagreed with other people?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they ignored them or looked down on them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What about religion?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My grandfather was very sincere in his beliefs, and brought my mother up that way. And the other grandfather was Scottish and Presbyterian. Grandfather Crees was Methodist no, I don't think he was involved in building the church here, but I wish I knew.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What happened following graduation in 1914?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, my Mother thought she had such a struggle in life when she was teaching school, that she didn't want me to work, so I fooled around here 4 years at home. Then started college, OAC, when my brother was old enough to go with me. I graduated in 1922, and got married the same year. I majored in Home Economics, which was the main thing for women in those days.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kinds of things did you do those 4 years at home?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just helped on the farm mostly. There was plenty of work to do. I think the hardest work I ever did was to help my father mow [pronounced to rhyme with cow] away a load of hay. It was so dusty and hot. I worked in the fields some and drove the horses to drive the machinery and I always drove the horse to pull up the hay, which is hitched to long rope and pulley. And the man on the load of hay has to put, push the hay fork into the bunch of hay up into the mow . . . and somebody in the mow spreads it around. It's something like real work.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are there any buildings related to families, other than the Crees?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, my father's house, which was built in two parts -- one in 1912 and the other a little later -- is still standing on the L. [Lloyd] Anderson place [Highland at Crescent Valley Dr.]. I lived there until 1922.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You talked about your mother's comments on teaching?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My mother, Kate Crees Gragg, taught in several places. I wish I knew all of them. She graduated from Monmouth Normal and then taught in Airlie, Eola Hills, Clatsop County, and a few other.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What were the difficulties?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, she had the old-fashioned idea that a girl should be at home and when she's grown, marry and have a family, and not be out working. And some of these schools, there were discipline problems and I remember her telling another young teacher, "Well, I would knock down and drag out." Now, you're not allowed to do it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was Corvallis like in the early years?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, Second Street was it! Corvallis in 1900 was a very small town. And Second St. was

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: the main street. There were no businesses on other streets for a while and no paving. Some of the dust was inches deep in the summer, and in the winter, the mud was inches deep.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How would you describe it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, where Albright and Raw is was a hardware store owned by the Smiths, who are still around. And across the Street was a livery stable . . . there were several. And I remember the Occidental Hotel about where the US Bank is. And the one saloon1 on Second Street, I think the building's still there. If you saw a drunk man, that ruined the whole day. The Opera House was built around the 1880's I think, where Safeway's old parking lot is. They had traveling companies of players and I remember our high school had a play there once. It was a big rectangular building and quite a landmark.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know the Kigers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. I lived on Kiger Island the first year I was married, and was a neighbor to Minerva's brother Dick. He had a peach orchard and I picked peaches off the back of a horse!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did Chatau qua come at all?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. It was a big tent at the lower end of campus. It was an educational kind of thing. I went with my fiance Phil Fleischman, and I don't remember the entertainment, but it was entertaining. . . there was variety. Everybody went, it was the thing to do.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did you do after you were married to Mr. Fleischman?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I stayed home and kept house and raised two daughters [Phyllis Dentel and Marjory Fitzwater}. One lives east of Lebanon and the other's at Oakridge.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When did you go to work?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I went in '41 when my husband died. I worked in the Seed Lab for 18 years. I was trained for 2 weeks to be a seed analyst.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever run into some Indians around here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the Indians were on Reservations by then. When I was a child, I'd see lots of Indians in the late summer and early fall during the hop picking season. Their dress was very colorful, and they'd sometimes sell baskets. My uncle traded a suit of clothes for a basket that I have in the Museum2.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have a lot of duties as a youngster?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, there was always plenty to do on the farm. All that stock had to be taken care of and fed, and watered. Therefore you had to raise and store feed for the winter. There's where your work came in. All the washing had to be done on a scrubbing board. Then my father bought one of the early washing machines . . . a little better; then he got one run by a gas motor. Then there was the canning . . . lots of fruit to can, and after we got a pressure cooker, we could can vegetables. And the meat was all hung and smoked, or put in heavy crocks cooked and covered with hot steaming lard. I also had to wash and clean Kerosene lamps . . . another little duty. George is my brother and he still owns quite a bit of the farm.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: [Footnote] The saloon was on the 2nd Street, Corvallis (c. 1900).

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: [Footnote] Bessie Murphy had her own museum behind her house.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Part II.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: August 4, 1975 Interview

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: [Interview conducted by Judy Carlson at Bessie Murphy's home]
bracketed_corrections: [Interview conducted by Judy Carlson at Bessie Murphy's home]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Could I hear a little bit more about your Scottish ancestry?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Gragg -- my father's people -- they came originally from Fishire to North Ireland in probably the early 1700's. And began coming to America before the Revolution, because some of them served in the Revolutionary War. Gradually, they began going West. I've got them back to Tennessee now and into Missouri, where my grandfather was born.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You 're very proud of your Scottish ancestry.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I am. My father had a lot of influence on me. I just wonder if parents and generations past didn't have more influence on their children than they do now, because life went along with a great deal of the same beliefs and ideas, and now it's so radically different.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What about Scottish characteristics?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, in general, the men were t11 and raw boned. They liked to keep family traditions, clear down to my time. One was about the uncle in the Putnams Army. One was a guard on the dock at Boston when ships came, and General Washington and his aides went down to the dockside to look through their spy glasses. Then Washington turned to my uncle and asked him if he didn't want to look, and he did, and he could see the buttons on the soldiers' uniforms. Now that's several generations ago! My father talked a lot about the ones he knew. I did visit the historical society in Belfast and learned some general history. If I had more time, I could have learned a lot more.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the Scottish trait of "watching your pennies"?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, there were very few of them that had any chance of making any big money, and they had to be careful with what they had.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And your father?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He was very economical, but he wasn't what you called tight. But there was more economy practiced in times past than there is now. Scotch and German and everything else were economical. The waste bothers me. And it's very, very unnecessary and makes our taxes high. And the taxes are exorbitant.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You've traveled a lot, haven 't you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Some, United States, Hebrides Islands. . Bonnie Prince Charlie Country, still full of . traditions. And some of the people would like to turn back the page of history to that time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you like to return to times past?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I personally would, but if the world will not learn from its mistakes, what's the use of going back?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What time would you return to?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When I was a child. I thought that was great. Automobiles were just coming in. The transition from the horse to the automobile. To me, the automobile didn't thrill me.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you still horseback ride?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not these days. Not for 20 years. My back bothers me, from a fall off a horse and arthritis.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You have so many other interests, what are they?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the latest is making colored slides of wild flowers. And I try to get them all in different areas, the coast, the valley, over in the desert, and I've just returned from a trip to the Wallowa Mountains. Lots of people enjoy seeing them, but it's just for my own use.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you still weave?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. And spin, and collect buttons. And I belong to the [Benton Co.] Historical Society. All these things give me contact with people. . and keep me on the map. As you get older and lose your old friends, you must get some new ones or you won't have any.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you visit with friends that you knew from your youth?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Minerva Kiger Reynolds is about the only one left. Our old neighbors were the Sol King family and the Withams, and there are a few descendants around. And I saw Lena Saxton yesterday, she was a high school friend. After my father died, my mother sold some of the property to the Lloyd Andersons. My brother still farms some of his land on the other side of Crescent Valley High School, although he lives in Monniouth. He camps there in the summer time when he's working on his garden. The property in front of the High School his where my father had is corn patch. That's where he plowed up the Indian relics.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ride into Corvallis on horseback when you were younger?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Seldom horseback. Horse and buggy usually.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are there outings you remember.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well always, we went to the fourth of July celebrations. That was a big red letter day. I'm sure sometimes the main events were on the courthouse lawn. And always, there was a patriotic speaker, and of course they had to get on some big open spaces where they could have merry-go-rounds and things like that. And all the little girls had to wear fancy white dresses with lace on it . . . and we had to be careful not to get them dirty. . . they were a nuisance to wash and iron.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did you wear horseback riding?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: At first I had a divided skirt, and later on a jodhpur type outfit. The turn of the century was the transition from side saddle to stride saddle.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And where did you hitch your horse in town?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, there were rings in the pavement and hitching racks in various places.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What stores stand out in your memory?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Dan Nolan off Second Street (Dept. store), and then he moved to Third. Mimer, who had candy and gum, on the south end of Second.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there a status difference between a farm child and a city child going to school?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I'm really not sure. I think it more depended on what you did -- how your grades were, and how you conducted yourself. Everybody had horses. Cars were fairly common by 1915.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What about early memories in the Crees house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. My grandfather retired and moved downtown by the time we came. I visited there [my aunt and uncle owned it for many years] but not my grandfather. I thought it was elegant.
bracketed_corrections: [my aunt and uncle owned it for many years]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How well do you remember your grandfather?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, well.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What is your philosophy of live. . . what keeps you going so actively?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it's partly my idea that you keep a-Ogain as long as you can. And do the best you can as you're going. I've always had a zest for life and I still have it, although I don't have the strength to go with it to do the things I'd still like to do. More travel for one thing. . . and a good garden.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are these ideas your parents had?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I think so. They were ambitious and tried to improve their farm. It's hard to put it in words.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about some of the clubs you belonged to at OSU?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I stayed at home, see. The Home Ec club and the Downtown Girls Club is all I remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think you majored in Home Ec because it was erpected of you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: More or less, yes. I'm not sorry although it might have been better if I could have done something else. There was a time, I think I could have indulged science, and gone in as a lab technician . . . I liked bacteriology and botany. At that time men were monopolizing science.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They still are.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I guess so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When did you start taking pictures of wildflowers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just last spring. I talked to friends and got advice, and the rest is luck. I'm lucky I have this friend who has a jeep -- that's the easy way to climb a mountain.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What about the bouncing?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I'm used to bouncing along on a farm wagon when I was a kid, and then on a horse. I liked the farm and all the activities on it. And I really liked the horses.

She said that her parents weren't really interested in plants, they had the belief or felt that most of plants are weeds since they were farmers that was their perceptions, but she did have some neighbors most of whom were girls and when she was a child she enjoyed going out with them and looking for plants and identifying plants. Over the years Bessie Murphy has been involved with several groups that enjoy going out and looking for plants in the forests and throughout this interview we spoke of places that she enjoys looking for plants. In this part of the interview that didn't tape very well, I asked Bessie Murphy about specific places that they looked for plants and what types of plants she felt were special, what were her favorites. They do not grow everywhere, they will only grow in real . . . very particular places and these . . . there's good areas to find a variety of orchids near Sulphur Springs that's in the McDonald Forest, the OSU Research Forest. She also mentioned Trillium plants as being some of her favorites, and specific genus species of couple types of trilliums were mentioned.]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so no, I got this set up better it will come out. . . the tape will record better, so we talked about several plants, the moccasin flower [Cpripedium montanum/ and the Trillium ovatum, is that what you called it, and then the one that you showed me, the how do you pronounce this one, Habernaria elegans.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Habemaria elegans, it's an orchid.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and spring beauty [Cardamine pulcherrima/, you said is the first one that blooms.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The first really pretty, interesting one that blooms in the spring other than little weeds, you know, they come first, some of them. And then of course there's bleeding heart [Dicentra formosal.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, that's one of my favorites.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And it has to have a wet place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And there's a little orchid, oh, what is that common name, calypso [Calypso bulbosa], it's a little pink one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Does that bloom around here, the calypso orchid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, if it's the right conditions, it will grow in this area. And look at the wild ginger [Asarum caudatum], isn't that interesting.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I've transplanted that in my yard and it grows.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They won't all do it, but that does. I've never monkeyed with the orchids, try to do anything with them, they're too touchy. Now this is another orchid, instead of a moccasin it's sort of a lip. And this is the same. And they grow up there in those woods around Sulphur Springs. Now this is a famous twin flower [jmaea borealis], the national flower of Switzerland.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And it's supposed to be pink.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Real light pink.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, light to medium pink and it's perennial on a little vine and these are called queen's cups [Clintonia uniflora]. They're a very interesting thing too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where are some other places that you liked to go out in the McDonald Forest to look for plants, or did you have any other special places?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just explore the place, you see, I haven't thoroughly explored it. I don't know what there is there any more, it's been so long since I could walk very far.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember much about what it is like anymore. It's awful strange, you see, it [Sulphur Springs] used to be a public campground, and I got over there and even my grandfather camped over there once with his family.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long would they stay, usually?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It depends on how long they have time to do it. Some of them would go over and stay a week, tents . . . there were tents, and everything.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I heard that and I was just wondering ,f they stay for over night or if it would be a week vacation, or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, for a few days, it depends on how long they'd be from home and how they liked it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I wonder what attracted people to that spot, why they liked that spot.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I think it was them springs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You think so?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were very popular in the early days, there's sulphur springs and soda springs, there's one at Sodaville.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It doesn't seem like there's much water coming out at Sulphur Springs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: On, no. That little pocket was always full.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. Is there as much water as there used to be in there, is it about the same?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The last time I saw it, it was. It isn't flowing much. You can dip it up and when . . at . various times, a person that owned it that I know of in 1900 was a Mr. Baker, Baker Creek was named for and he had it fixed up really nice and he had a croquet grounds and I don't think he did it but somebody later on cemented up the spring and had a cement thing there at the water come up like a fountain, you know. And of course vandals, they had to ruin it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Sickening. And then during the War [World War II] the army, the men did a lot of work over there and put up tables and all kinds of things, you know, and for . . . and that was about the time my girls were big enough . . oh, teenagers, and we did lots of horseback . riding. We'd go over there horseback riding all around. We'd go over there and take our lunch and oats for the horses and we'd pour the oats on the table and they ate them off the table. Well, the vandals ruined that. It's just maddening. Fools.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did you keep your horses?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We had them at home.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you rode all the way.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, we lived on Kings Road, we took them over the hills.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there any logging roads up there then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember of any logging, there may have been some but it wasn't prominent.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It. . . was it a farm. . . who owned that land, that forest then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The valley itself has the farm land and it was being farmed by farmers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What about up the slopes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, that was just wild country as far as I know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Because that was. . might have been Universily. . . some of it might have been donated to the . University by then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Might have been, I don't know that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I heard that it might have been Mr. Baker used to take his cattle from Soap Creek over to Oak Creek across the hill there right by Sulphur Springs.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. I understand that he did. And then there was one or two other men that were businessmen that lived over there at that time. There was one Mr. Moore who used to have . later had a chicken hatchery in Corvallis, and I went to school with his children. They lived there and farmed there for some years before they went to town. But it's a small valley and it isn't the best land.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: For farming?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. Well, tell me about Dimple Hill3. I've heard that that is a nice spot for looking for wild flowers.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. It used to be. It's mostly unforested. It's bare, you know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, it's a meadow.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A natural meadow.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And at that time it was owned by old timers here by the name of Locke. An area full of them. And it was called Locke Hill. And I don't think it is fair for some modern smart alec to come along and change the name. That was named for an old timer, pioneer. Of course, the Dimple Hill was done by just everybody because it looked like dimples, those ravines looked like dimples.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: [Footnote] The "Dimple Hill" Bessie is referring to is 'Chip Ross Park. It was called "Dimple Hill" before "IV Hill" before Chip Ross Park. It is thought that he name Dimple Hill was accidentally transferred to the old "Jackson Hill" by an error of U.S. Geological Survey. This is also known as "Mitzie Point" named after a surveyors dog who died at this location.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And it was called Dimple Hill

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But before that it was called Locke Hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, oh always, from the beginning.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Have you heard the name Mitzie Point?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What's that anyway?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They call. . . some people call Dimple Hill, Mitzie Point.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that's some personal thing they know about that I don't. And then it was named for this boy that got killed, I guess, it was Chip Ross.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, yeah, that's on the other side of Dimple Hill, the Chip Ross Park.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, you see we lived up against this west. . . east side, my father's farm came up that far against the Hill, or Locke Hill, whatever you want to call it. But I've noticed that lately, a good many years, there'd be some pioneer feature of the country called by a pioneer name for years and years then moderns come in and rearrange everything and change the names. I don't think it's smart.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. Are there any other points or places in the forest that you remember a name for that. what about McCulloch Peak, has that always been called McCulloch Peak?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I've never heard of that. I don't know where it is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It's west of Oak Creek, it's up this way going towards Kings Valley, Kings Valley would be out here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Little out of my range. I didn't go there with a horse.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think you had. . . your own names for places you went to when you went horse riding.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, yes, somewhat just for us so as to mark what it is, so you could tell directions.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What about Oak Creek, did you. . . do you ever spend any time looking. . . is Oak Creek a placed that you would go to look for special plants?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let me see now, where is Oak Creek?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's where you go by the fish lab, you get. . there's a few buildings that OSU has.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, out west of town?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. I've forgotten the area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Kind of by the fairgrounds there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we didn't go out there much. It was quite a ways to go and we had plenty of other ways.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So Sulphur Springs was a place you went. Do you ever go up around Lewisburg Saddle and look for plants at all with your friends?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let me see now, what's that?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's where there's. . . you go over the crest on the way out to Sulphur Springs and.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah, that was our main trail, see, the Sulphur Springs Road and the Sulphur Springs area and the close by the hills.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: All in there, huh?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, because you don't want to just ride all day, you want to do something. And the horses got tired.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you'd look for plants for a while and get off?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And we did climb Vinyard's Hill, but not with the horses. But we had to climb those hills, that was something to do.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So then was Vinyard Hill up behind. . . where Vinyard Estates is now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's the tallest hill over in there, and it's bare on the front.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And they have the TV tower up there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I believe so. And you see, it was named. . . partly owned by the old time family, Vinyards, and the original Vinyard, was a teacher at the College.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember what he taught?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, that was before my time. A son and his family lived there on the hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about Peavy Arboretum, do you ever these days. . . do you ever go to the Arboretum and look for plants or any areas in there . . . are there any good spots in there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember, I don't do so much of it anymore. And I can't go unless somebody takes me because I'm too old to drive. I'm handicapped. I miss all this.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about Jackson Creek, do you know where.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, you bet your life.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Because that was closed to your family farm.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I came through my father's place

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wow!

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right down by the high school. And Frazier Creek north of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right. There 's a cabin up in there, in the forest.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There is? I didn't know that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, a log cabin, there's two of them, and they're all. . . nobody lives in them, they're just tiny little things, I think they were built when the conservation corps were Out there, the army people.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes, it could be.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there was afarm up there, up Jackson Creek, there's an old farmhouse up there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes, that was the Stonebacks. Our neighbor, George Stoneback. If it's the one I think it is. He was up there, he wasn't on the Jackson place, he was north of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Maybe I'm thinking of Jackson place.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Maybe. Yeah, there's several Jackson brothers and some. . I don't know if they all . or all . . . but there's two especially, I think they were bachelors and they evidently lived in town because they come out through the trail to go to the place, they'd walk along single file on the trail and come out to the place to do something, because they didn't live there anymore. You see, I was pass . . . they were. . . when they lived there and their parents and all, I wasn't there yet, I didn't know that. All I knew of them was those old men. And they didn't live by us.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was your maiden name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Gragg.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How do you spell it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: G-r-a-g-g.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and how many acres was your family farm there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Supposed to be 200 about that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you raise cows, did your parents raise cows?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, it was general farming.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, a little bit of everything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A little bit of everything. And there was a lot of that, you see that's what most of the country consisted of was small farmers at that time. And it gave them a chance to make a living and didn't have to be beggars. I think it was a whole lot better than the way it is now. It just makes me sick, no farmers anymore. It's a mess now, all these farmers, their kids as they grow up and teenage times, there's always something for them to do, especially during the harvest season, there was hop picking. And different fruit picking. And. . . I'm trying

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: to think But there was ever so many things that these children could do and earn their money and help them in school and everything like that. Now there's nothing in those, don't amount to anything. I imagine there's a little fruit picking in the fall, maybe. But it's entirely different. I saw a lot of things change. Ask me more questions if you've got them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, the main thing I was interested in is places on the forest. What. . . any stories you knew about and you 'ye given me some really good infonnation about where people had their farms and the Jackson place and the Stonebac/cs and Locke Hill, that's the kind of stuff I'm looking for.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was the farthest west that there was any agriculture. Mr. Stoneback and Jacksons. And

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, what kind ofjobs did you have, you said you worked at a. . . something about seeds?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, you mean me?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I was . . . do you know how a seed lab functions?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, you see there's lots of grain raised in Oregon but not necessarily this side of the mountains, it's over in Eastern Oregon, big grain fields and all. And whatever's raised that is sold has to be tested for quality. And that's what we did. They'd measure out a certain amount, by weight of those seeds, different kinds of seeds you see had different amounts, and we had to go through them with a lens and see everything in them. All the other seeds, weed seeds, everything, and estimate the amount of junk in them and all that before it was sold, so they could be told what the quality was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's still the seed lab.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've seen people working on campus.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, you bet. I don't think there's as much as there used to be. There used to be quite a lot of people. But the last one that I knew is retiring this week. And I think most of those that worked with me, you see, I've been retired thirty years. Most all the others are gone, they aren't all, but most of them are gone.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many years did you do that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Seventeen.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And how many kids do you have?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Two.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, two daughters.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And how many grandkids?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Four, and I've got three great grandchildren.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There's no public roads. We couldn't even get over to those. . . And what do you want me to say about the right-of-way. What it is?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You were telling me about something about petitioning the county.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's to get the county road. We had to use a right-of-way before there were any county roads. And that's just going through. . . there's a law allowing you to go through your neighbors place if you have no other way to get out, but you have to go where he says you can go on his place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And what year was that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was 1900.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Boy it is hard to imagine how different things were then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, you see it from that angle, I see it from the other end.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. How much it has changed.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes! Well, then about the county road, in 1905 the neighbors petitioned the county court to get. . . to make them a road, to open them up a public road. And they said, "Sorry, we have no funds for a road." So then like a little red hen they said, "We'll do it ourselves." And that was something.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: All the neighbors went together and built a road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Went together except one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They worked all summer long, all they possibly could on that. I tell you it was something, I saw the whole thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And what road would that be today, is there a road there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Highland Way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Really? Wow!

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That would. . . that is pretty steep hill even going over Highland.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You bet it is, it is. Coming up to it both ways from. And of course they had to go around then and get permission from the owners where to put the road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And all the owners gave permission?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: All but one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And what did you do about that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we had to pay him

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. Did he use the road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, some.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He probably did eventually.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, but he soon moved away, nobody was sorry. But they had to go, you see, to all Highland Way clear down to Kings Road and had to get permission from those people, one of them was my grandfather, my maternal grandfather, of course he gave the road for mama's sake.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And what was his name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Crees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's the Crees House, you told me.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. There was ever so many people, you see, because it was quite a little. . . it was about three . . . at least three miles. And they didn't . . . some people grumbled about it, the road, but they couldn't get any where else, they had . . . the people make it had to take what they got and the owners and do the best that they could.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And then when they got the road done and a little bit of gravel on and fixed up so they could use it. That fall I came to town to school on my pony.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Really? How long did it take you to get to school?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's farther now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And wasn't school where the park is today, by the library?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It's Central Park.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Central Park.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes. So. . . I'm just curious, what did you do with your pony tied up while you were in class?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, you know, at that time, that was in 1905, not nearly all the people had a car and lots of little barns in town.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you have to pay like to keep your pony at a barn?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A little bit because papa had to haul in hay and stuff to feed it. Yeah, but after a few years all the barns were gone or made into something else. I'm sure cars made the biggest change in civilization there's been for quite a while.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think it would be neat to ride horses instead of driving cars. It would be cold.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, it had drawbacks, but it has pleasure and fun. And you had to learn something too. I loved it. And let's see, the. . . and because the county didn't have the money, you see, we could . . . they couldn't make a road. But the individual little things that . . . one that will interest you the next door neighbors was named Witham and that's an old timer out south of town, it was one of the Witham boys that lived there, family. And they had a on their place was a fairly level place. . . spot that was not trees and the wild strawberries were just thick, and this was in May when they were working on the Witham part. And just as the strawberries were coming, getting ready to be picked, and Mrs. Witham was about to cry because they were going to work on her part that day and ruin the strawberries, so the men got their heads together and said they'd work somewhere else till she could harvest her strawberries.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Boy, all these names, Witham Hill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was all families.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You bet, old timers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. That's great. It gives so much more meaning to everyday things.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You know where the names came from.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it called Crescent Valley then? Would you.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: For a long time it wasn't called anything I think. I don't know . . . I don't remember what it was called. I don't believe it was called, for some time at least.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just the valley north of town. One of the valleys. Well I don't want to keep you any.
