entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We 're at the home of Bessie Murphy, north of Corvallis and doing an interview and the first question I would like to ask you is when you first moved to Corvallis and why you moved here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I moved in 1900 with my family when they left Clatsop County and came here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And where did you first move to?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Crescent Valley Farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And who owned the farm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Heavens, I don't know. I was only five years old.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did your father buy it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, he bought it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see and then was he a full time farmer?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What crops did he raise?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, in those days, we didn't just specialize in one crop. It was a family farm that we raised everything, we were self sufficient on the farm. And he raised hay for the horses and cows and some grain, wheat mostly at first and oats and then we had a garden which was a great deal of our food, because a lot of things we could keep for through the winter.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall the names of the farmers that lived adjacent to you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes, the one of the west was Old Witham and he was from an old time family.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was he living on the William donation land claim?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know about that. I wouldn't be surprised, but I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was he the same type of farmer, self sufficient?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. And then going still farther west, there was one by the name of George Stoneback. He had a little . . . rather hilly little farm and he didn't have very big variety of crops and then to the east toward the highway, there were several different ones that ended up with the Holbrook family. And my brother bought it from them. At that time we were grown. And he bought that from Mrs. Holbrook. Her husband died.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How big were these farms?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Papa's was 200 [acre] and the Holbrooks were 50, the Witham was probably 200 or more and Stoneback was probably 100.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall the farms to the North?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not so good.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any families in the Soap Creek Area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Say the Marc/cs or the Olsons.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I've heard of them, but I didn't know them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Wiles.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I've heard of all of those.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Carters?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wouldn't know the Carters.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, your adjacent neighbors were the people that you knew best?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you know anyone from the Locke family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, we knew them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did the Witham or the other families that you mentioned have children your age?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, the Witham girl was older than me. Then on the south toward town was the King family from the Kings Valley family.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Solomon King's family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Sol's descendants. And that was a large family. And I started out with them when I first went to school, there was a little school down on the highway. One little building and we all went there. Had to walk. . . I had to walk two miles.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the name of that school?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Sunnyside.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Sunnyside School?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It's not there anymore is it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. No, in about two years the district. . . was taken into the city district, town district and I had to go there and then I had to go three and half miles, so I got to ride my pony.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What happened to the Sunnyside School?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was made into a private home. . . residence. But that wasn't the original, the original was torn down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the Sunnyside School you were going to was a newer school and then after they stopped using it they turned it into somebody's home?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then what happened to it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, you see when I first went there it was a little old pioneer version of it, it was just a little one room building.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About 1907 or 1908?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, before that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was six in 1900 and I started school when I was seven and that was torn down and the new one was built and then two years later it was taken into the city.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. Then when you went to school, you had to walk those two miles?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there a road or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No road in those days.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just across the fields?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You bet. You go on somebody's right of way, there were right of ways. You had to go where the owners said you bad to go.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So if somebody made a diagonal across their field or they made you follow a fence line..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was naughty.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You could destroy crops or get muddy or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Get into trouble.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How come you didn't ride your pony to Sunnyside School?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I didn't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why not, too many fences?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. And I didn't have a pony then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did anybody run cattle or anything that would make it kind of dangerous going across certain

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember any cattle, but that was a hazard. No, when I went to town to school, I rode the pony.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the pony's name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Belle.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long did you have her?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Years and years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the whole time you went to school you rode Belle to school when you went to town?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember when you graduated?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: From high school in '14.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then. . let's see f I recall, you worked at home for a few years before you went to college?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: . Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When did you start college?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm not so good on dates.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it a four-year degree?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think I stayed home four years from high school to college; that would have been '18 or '19 I started to college.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: During World War I?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I guess it was. But I don't remember all of these.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall what you did on the farm for fun when you were a young girl?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I jumped on that pony and went all over the place, explored, went to Sulphur Springs and around the hills That was my main fun.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the main route to Sulphur Springs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Lewisburg Road, that's the only road here when we came. The public road. All the rest were right of ways. And then you see in 1905, '04 or '05, the community put in Highland Way. Then we could get to town without right of ways and gates.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Before Highland Way was put in was there a road or a track in that general area already?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. Just right of ways.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they line up into similar alignment to what was

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we couldn't go on Highland Way, there was no way. We went down to the highway here where the school is. . was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the name of the highway at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The right of ways didn't have names

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No when you went to the highway.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, ninth street.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was the highway. Was it called ninth Street?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. That's the way we left town on ninth street.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that. . . did you go through where the Owens. . . what was it, Applegate?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I'll tell you that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you go through that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Owens on this side of us, Mr. William Knotts was the owner and resident there. And Owens was one of his children or grandchildren or great grandchildren . . . child owns it now. And we . . . he let us have a route through his place for awhile on a certain place and he changed it. And that went along the fence from the corner of my father's place on Highland Way but before Highland Way got put in, we went down to the highway, the line of Mr. Owens'

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: fence on the south side of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the south boundary?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Where the opposite the property where the hospital is on the south side of it, as you go out ninth street a little way, I mean the highway here, as you go out there and come to that ridge.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That the hospital is on?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, the other side of the hospital, along the line of the fence, of the Knotts place or the Owens now. You can still see the tracks going west along the fence and turning to the right or south, you can see that turn just before you get to the highway.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Those are the tracks that preceded Highland Road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And those. . . that would be the main route to town. . . before 1905.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. That was the right of way that we had a right to go on.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would all that south traffic have a right of way on that or was that an east - west route.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's east - west.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did that have a name to it, that right of way or just called it the. . .?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You just call it by the name of the owner of the property.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Owens right of way.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And those tracks are still there

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: and they predate 1905?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not 1905, they don't predate it, they date that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When was the last that those tracks were used?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well it probably was 1905, but the road didn't get put in so it could . . . it was usable that first year that they made it, only in spots. Little sections. Yes, probably 1906 until that old right of way was dumped.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that the remains of that right of way, that you know?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's all you can see, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you pay much attention to when they stopped using a road how maybe the vegetation filled in, what types of plants began growing in the old road or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I was more or less observant of it because I was interested in it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you kind of describe what you noticed with that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, weeds and grass come pretty soon. And the nice flowers like spring beauties that he has a picture of, they didn't. . . they were a little more delicate and harder to do anything I mean, they are more liable to be not able to compete with the bad stuff, weeds and things.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are you calling weeds, exotic plants brought into the area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Weeds, some of the wild mustards, and things in the daisy family and buttercups and dandelions and those things. They are very prolific and they take over.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you went to Sulphur Springs, was that just a destination a place to turn around and come back or did you do things when you got there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, you see that was a public picnic ground because of the springs. Public used it quite a bit in those days. Went there and camped. It was considered . . . you see, that was very in those days the natural mineral springs were very popular. And this wasn't so popular because people didn't like water so well, it's the soda springs that were popular.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are there any soda springs around here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not right around here. There's one at Cascadia, it's just where they were, but people did camp here. When we came here in 1900, that summer I remember my grandfather and his family was out there camping at those springs {Sulphur Springs]. And we went over there and visited one Sunday.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long would people camp --for a day or two or week?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, they'd camp a week.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they do anything besides drink the water?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what they did. I explored of course, that's what I'd do, and I did drink the water because I thought if I came that far I should drink some of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't care for the taste too well.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It must of helped you, you're pretty healthy several years later. That's what they always claimed would happen.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Maybe that's the secret of it, I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Maybe we'll get more people going there to drink the water now.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Grandpa had a tent and was camping there and of course, when we went there was no such a thing as a car at that time so we had to go with a surrey with a fringe on top and two horses and that was quite a trip over that Sulphur Springs Hill, it's pretty rugged, pretty rough.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Had that road been in for quite awhile?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Could people take bicycles over the road or would they hike in without buggies?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. All kinds of ways or they'd go horseback.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would very many people be there at one time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There were quite a few that Sunday, I remember, camping.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When. . . who 's land was Sulphur Springs located on?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think I've read about that but I don't remember. I know there was one man who owned by the name of Baker. I just can't remember the names.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they have any kind of camping tables or structures?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember of it, there may have been, but he did have. . . one of those people that had it, I don't know if it was Baker or not, but he had fixed up a croquet grounds.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would that be where the meadow still is, maybe?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. I think so. And then when the army was here [WW II, Camp Adair], they had fixed up quite a bit. I remember there were big tables, when we'd go there horseback we'd feed our horses oats on the table.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you don 't remember any houses or structures of that variety there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I can't. That's not to say there might not have been.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about at the Springs, some people say that there used to be a concrete fountain there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Vandals broke it up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know how. . . about how tall that fountain was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, as I remember it was as tall as this table.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About three feet?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did it have much force? Right now it just barely bubbles out of the ground.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it just bubbles out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there any benches or anything built around the fountain?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, no, but there was some benches and tables and things when the army was here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Around the fountain?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not around the fountain, near the fountain.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was the field any larger at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember about that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The hills, did they look any different?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No,

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About the same?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: About the same.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there. . . was the timberline, the meadow line on those hills facing west. . . do you recall if that was any different or have you noticed any changes through time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't remember of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it's always, for the last ninety-five years it's been about the same?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's reassuring. How about the plants in the field, have you noticed many changes in those plants?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. There was lots of interesting wild flowers in the area and I'd go around and spot some of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are they still there, most of them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that area has pretty stable variety of grasses and flowers through time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I would say it has. And there was some there that are more or less rare like the. what's the name of that, there were several orchids, but I was think of that one . . it's in the buttercup family, oh, shucks. I can't think of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: If that area's now starting to be used more again, it's stopped for a number or years, and now people are starting to botanize in the forest more, that's what Marlene [Finley] was working on. Do you think it's a good idea for some of those plants that aren't too common to be identified and have people look at them or do you think it's better just to avoid those areas and try to keep that infonnation privileged?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I just wouldn't know, because so many times they end up. . . people don't understand how to take care of them and they end up being ruined.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think f there were signs there to tell them that this is a rare plant, don't ruin it, that this would be good or bad?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it all depends on the person, some people would dig it up and take it home and of course, it would never, practically never, live.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: One of the things I was hoping to ask is plants that were rare or unusual in this area where you've seen them or maybe they've been exculpated or maybe where they are still there, but I'm also, since other people will be able to see this maybe it's not a good idea to identify exact locations [people would misuse the information.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's the trouble, there's always somebody that spoils it all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Have you seen any plants in the Soap Creek area or Sulphur Springs or Dimple Hill or. . . you call it, Locke Point?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Locke Hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any plants that you've seen in those areas that maybe aren't so common anymore or maybe disappeared?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. You know, the Sisyrinchium doglasu....grass lily,yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: If you use Latin that's all right, Phil [Hays] is the interpreter.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Have either one of you been up the Columbia Gorge in the spring when they're thick. thousands of them . . . just thick masses of those?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes, but I've never noticed them.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that's too bad because I only saw two in my lifetime in this area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you haven't seen any. . . have you seen any recently?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the name of them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's a grass lily, it's a dainty thing that the leaves are much like grass, it's kind of flat. And the lily is about an inch or little better in diameter, I think, and on a little a dainty little stem and the wind. . . any little breeze will make it shake and it's very dainty and pretty. I'd call it a . . . I think it's a different name for it's a color. It ought to be, but I don't know what they call it. To me it was purple.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: More of a crimson?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not crimson.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Purplish red.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's beautiful and dainty, and I don't know why it's so scarce here. If two of them could grow why couldn't more.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall where they were located?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, you bet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you want to put it into the record? Maybe you'd get more people looking for them and find some, got some clues.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: One was on the road going to Sulphur Springs in the south and bare face of that hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Of Lewisburg Saddle?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Hill. Is that hill still bare today, the same area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know whether the trees have covered it or not. I've noticed that some of those bare spots on those hills are not so bare, the trees are closing in a little.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What do you think about that, do you think that's endangering plants by having those trees move into those bare areas?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes, because the plants out there in the bare part, can't be happy in dense forests.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, what would your preference be, f you owned that land would you start taking those trees out of there and making room for the plants or do you think that the trees are worth it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The trees are worth it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What's the reason? Why do you prefer the trees over the

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I don't prefer them. I'd just as soon have the flowers myself.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But it were your land, you 'd still have trees on it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'd probably leave it like it is. And the other one was in my father's field, one corner of the field had not been cleaned out and made into a crop. And it was in there, at the edge of that in the grass at the edge of that field where it got plenty of sun.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it's a plant that requires a lot of sunlight?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, it don't want to have any shade at all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: In your father's field, that would be flat moist area and up on the.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it was on a little hill, it wasn't perfectly flat.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Southern exposure again?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Southeast exposure, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So a real dry area and sunny?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Dry for the Willamette Valley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, is that area, is that hill still there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, but it's made into a field.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It's been plowed since then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. That's where I . . that was sad for me. .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When they plowed that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Because that was the only one except the one on the hill that I ever saw, and nobody could think when they were cleaning that corner out to take that plant up on a shovel with a lump of dirt and plant it somewhere else.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: One thing I'm hoping to accomplish with that is to ma/ce sure that those lypes of things don't happen accidentally again, f there are plants that are rare or endangered, particularly in the forest or on the crop lands or on the highway right of ways, that we can recognize those locations. The one on the hill, that would have been along the old grade, the one that was used in.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was off the road, it wasn't on the road, but I went up there on my pony on the road and then I went off to investigate that hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that hill would have been to the west?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, southwest from the road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Southwest. Did you ever go back there looking for that plant?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think so, but I don't remember particularly when I left all that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any other plants that you noticed that aren't here anymore?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we all know, Phil and I and a lot more of them that these strawberry pinks [Silene hookeri] are getting very, very scarce. There used to be more of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And Phil knows where those are located now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Oh, yeah, we should speak of the orchids, they were especially prevalent over at Sulphur Springs. . . around Sulphur Springs. And one Cypripedium montanum. somebody, people [Smiths] we know out south of town actually got them to grow in their yard and they're doing wonderful. By the way, I've got a picture.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Cypripedium.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Large orchid.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you've got some pictures?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I might have to describe these in the microphone because. . and that's the one we're just discussing. That's Florence Smith's, would that be related to Greenberty Smith or Joseph Smith, Alexander Smith?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. They're old timers out there, Van could tell you, her husband.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] It's that corner of Smith Loop and Highway 99W, a white house there. Okay, so that's south of town, near Greenberry.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Now you see these have stems about, wouldn't you say, about a foot and a half high? And they have big leaves like this and you see the long.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: These used to grow out at Sulphur Springs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do they still grow out there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, because I can't go anywhere.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see, you '11 leave that up to me and Phil to look for them.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And the blossoms have this big. . . pouch like a moccasin. And it has purple veins, these leaves . . . these veins, these are parallel veins . . . leaves, that's how you describe a leaf like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now this is still growing out at the Smith's now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, in their yard near a big maple tree, but not too heavily shaded by it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So we could take and possibly reintroduce these back to Sulphur Springs if they 'ye been removed?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, but there's not much use.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why not?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they'll disappear by some vandal.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. Do you recall other plants in the neighborhood that you looked at, that through time became scarce or disappeared?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. I can't remember their names. I was going to tell you this other orchids . . but . that is the best one, that is the most beautiful one they have in Oregon. There's one up in the. . . now here's what happens to things, up here on the little hill of the old cemetery.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Locke Cemetery?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Locke Cemetery Hill There's an orchid that instead of having and being big like this and having a beautiful flower, it was a slender little stem about this high.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About afoot?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. And it was put. . .the flowers were put on the stem so they looked like. . . see if I can fmd it, smell that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Skunk cabbage.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Here we are, and here's the other orchid, I believe that's right side up, isn't it, Phil. Oh, see they're put on like cross stitch, that's interesting.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Habernaria elegans.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Habernaria elegans. That's one on my list, I think.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And anyway they grow up there, and they're not as fussy about where they grow as these and in the spring, early in the spring . . early before decoration day, I've been up there and . I saw one growing between an edge of a plot, but when I went back on decoration day, the caretaker had mowed if off.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Will that kill the plant?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, no it may not, but it's pretty hard on it to take all its leaves.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall the plot it was next to?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was near my brother's. Well, you see they don't teach about nature to kids anymore, or even high schoolers. People ought to know more about these, they ought to be taught more.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, one thing we're trying to do with this information is take kids out in the forest and find some of these plants that you 're going to describe, so I think they think the same thing as you, that they ought to teach them more.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But how can they make an intelligent decisions about anything that has to do with plants if they don't know anything?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You've got me. You're preaching to the choir.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I'm kind of irked about some of those things.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, the three of us here. . . did they used to teach botany, did they used to teach.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I took it in high school.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And they took you out in the field and showed you the plants?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, not very much of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about when you went to college, did they do better?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes, that was better. Doc [Helen M.] Gilkey was my teacher.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He would take you out on field trips?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes, we went on field trips.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where would the field trips be?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Most anywhere around.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Sulphur Springs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Probably did go there once, I don't remember for sure.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you look mostly at flowers or trees or grasses?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was mostly plants, and she took us on longer trips to sometimes4.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Overnight?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not that way. There's the pink I've been talking about.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, that's pretty. What's it called?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Silene hookeri. I think I've got that one on my list too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] If you ever run across one you'd know it. Are they . . . have you seen them

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] I've never seen a picture that did justice.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I haven't either.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This is a red dot?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: See the little red dot?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Where's my
