entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You see you hold this up to your eye and you bring this up and when it's just right, you can see real . . [referring to Mimulus alsinoides]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where are these located at?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Where is that place

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] You took those out on Alsea Road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are there any local here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm not sure. I'm not sure.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, Phil was saying these used to be on Dimple Hill [referring to Silene hookeril

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not this. This is the one down here in the valley.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] It's [Silene hookeri] on the hill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It is? Fine. This other one [Sisyrinchium douglasiil is about this high.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About a foot.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And the blossom hangs over like a bell. This [Silene hookeri] doesn't, this is up flat, its face is up to the light. Grows differently.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is it pretty rare?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. You bet it is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know where any plants are.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I used to when I was growing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Was the pink [Silene hookerif real common down in the valley then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, but not thick. But it was much more common than it is now.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: [Footnote] We had flowers on the table as we talked.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What do you think caused it to be removed?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, part of it was the making fields out of the pastures, plowing it up, that's one thing. And another way's eliminating the place where it grows, I don't know what all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: If. . . so in areas where people are plowing, do you think certain areas should be maybe set aside to let some of these plants return or do you think they could return?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it's very . . . do you want to see these Phil? This one here is a spring flower. And it's leaves are edible.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is this a spring beauty?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Some of them call it that, but it isn't supposed to be. What do I call it?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What should I start calling it? Call it a Montia pefoliara.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Perfoliata.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Perfoliata?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, it's a different family The real spring beauties [Cardamine pulcherrima} that are in the mustard family. . . cabbage family and this is a different family, can't think what it is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This grows in the west side fairly common, doesn 't it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, it grows in my yard. It's easy.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] It's called miner's lettuce [Montia perfoliara.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's it. I was trying to think of it. Miner's lettuce and this is edible, leaves are very edible.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are you familiar with any of the plants maybe that the Indians used for food?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You bet, you bet. That's one of my . . oh, where's .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did you get the information that the Indians used them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Mostly out of a book.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So f somebody had a good reference book as far as what the Indians used, they would have the same information you had?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Here it is, there's the famous bitter root [Lewisia rediviva] of the Indians.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's bitter root.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And it doesn't grow in this side of the mountains.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just the east side?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just where it's dry.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the soap plant that's in Southern Oregon, could Soap Creek have been named after the Soap plant? Are you familiar with that plant?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I've just heard of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But not around here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, do you know anything about it?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever study any of the grasses, the native grasses?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are they still fairly common?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, there are some native grasses yet, but you see the farmers have brought in so many foreign crops of grasses -- just changed things like ever and they spread.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think there's a way to keep those grasses from spreading or do you think it's all right that they're spreading?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, might as well spread, they're good grasses.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Don't they create a lot of competition for the native grasses or the wildflowers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. Yes, they do.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you don't think that's a particular problem?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, you can't help it that I know of.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you have just become resigned to their fate?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's the word.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, how about some of the areas that they are managing for timber or they are using for pasturage, if they used different practices, maybe if they didn't plow or rotated crops would that be a way to encourage or retain some of these plants?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I suppose, I don't think they do much plowing, do they? I don't think they do.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I don't farm.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't believe they do much plowing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So when they plowed before, it wasn't a real frequent thing, is was just enough to disturb the.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: From the top of the ford was a field that was being put into crops.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they 're not growing so many crops anymore?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. You know what's happened to the family farm, don't you?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Getting extinct.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And that's too bad.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You think that's a better living situation for people, the family farm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it was certainly better for poor people, than being on charity.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You had to work like a horse.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they do any poaching in this area to supplement their diet or would they. . . was it strictly growing crops and.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, you see there were seasons that you could shoot pheasants and grouse and deer and things and they were more plentiful and the wild geese and all of that. And they had some of that. But on a family farm, you had a great variety of crops including chickens, and geese, and lots of things to eat.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you weren't dependent on wild game or fish to supplement your diet?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, and you could raise things in the garden like beans and peas and corn for hominy and all those things that you could keep through the winter. And then can what you couldn't keep dry.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think family farms. . . are there too many people today to have them, or do you think it would be good to have family farms maybe just so.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I certainly do, and have a sensible class to teach the children a little bit of agriculture and include a little botany.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So would you do that at high school level or college level?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, high school if not eighth grade, the younger you catch them the better you can do.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, after you got out of college, what did you do then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, for a couple of years, I guess it was, I stayed on the farm and helped the folks and then I got married.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: After you got married, where did you live?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we lived first on Kiger Island and I guess we just. . . oh, I think my husband had his job then, worked at the post office.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, your husband worked for the post office?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And he didn't have time to really farm, but we always had a garden.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So on Kiger Island.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was good ground, wow!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have any trouble with flooding?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, not much then that I remember of. Of course, there were some times when there was too much water over the road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you. . . no problem with your landlords or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not that I remember of.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long did you live at Kiger Island?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not more than two years I don't think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then where did you move?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Then we moved to . . . some property that my mother had, my grandfather had. That's where I ended up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: North of Corvallis?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then you remained your married lfe at that location?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, my husband [Phillip G. Fleischman] died young though and then I had to go to work. And I went to work with something that I could with my botany. I went to work at the seed lab.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have any children?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I had two daughters.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you were raising two daughters by yourself?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And working at the seed lab?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was your job there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Test the seed samples that come in, you have to test them for what the weed seeds are in what other kinds of crops and the percentage of all of those.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you had to identify the seeds and count the numbers and figure out percents.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, one of the workers did the percentages. My part was to just figure out what. identify all that was in the sample.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever notice any trends through time as you start getting more of certain types of weeds or cleaner grass seed?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, yes, we got different stuff and that was something that would come in and hadn't been here naturally. But I don't remember any particular one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did anybody keep records of that, what years that certain types of seeds started.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they may have, I don't know, they should have, but I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know who would know? Do you still have contacts at the seed lab and they could look at old records?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. I could. If I could do it I would.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'm willing to do it, I'm young and I've got time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: All right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You 'd have to give me a name or two names.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I'll give you some names

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, just don't want to do it for the record? Maybe somebody younger than me will listen to this tape and they'll get excited about it. Do you recall any names or Phil would you know who to check?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well who ever. . .1 don't go back and visit at the seed lab, I don't know what's going on now, but I know some of the older ones are getting older. I attest to that. But the. . . who

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: was the manager then is still living and she'd be a good one to ask.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What's her name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She's Mrs. Jensen, Louise Jensen . . . Louisa Jensen. Can't think of her husband's first name.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is she still here in town?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. You can fmd her in the phone book.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. When. . you said when you were younger you used to go out to Sulphur Springs, what

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: other places would you go with your horse?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that's about far enough, but I have made longer trips out. . . like I'd go out south of town and visit some friends that were farther than that. I'd have to stay over night though.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you go around Dimple Hill or Coffin Butte?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember that I ever did, I suspect that the fences kind of hindered that. I don't know why I never did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you call it Dimple Hill? I've heard it call it Mitzie Points, I think, and you called it Locke Hill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, you see he was the man who owned it when we first came here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Locke?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. And he bought a strip of land off of the south end of my father's place to have a road [Lester Ave.] in. So we had the little dillies with that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] Now, is that the one that was also called 1V6 Hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it's had all kinds of names?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] Chip Ross Park now.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, but that was Locke's Hill, that's all we knew it as when I was a child.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And now it's Chip Ross Park?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any of the other hills around here that their names may have changed or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, this biggest one out here was Vinyard's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Vinyard's Hill or Vinyard's Mountain?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just called hill then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about Bald Hill, did they call it another name other than Bald Hill, like old Ba/dy or. . . do you recall?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't recall. They were usually named for the person who owned the most property on them like that. That's why Locke's Hill is called that and Vinyard's Hill was called that after Mr. Vinyard, he was a professor at the college.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it wasn't named after a crop it was named after a person?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about Soap Creek, between Soap Creek and Berry Creek where they've got. . . called Smith

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: [Footnote] The current "Dimple Hill" was called "Jackson Hill" when Bessie was a child. What she calls "Locke Hill" was also called "Dimple Hill." It was called "IV Hill" later, and then became Chip Ross Peak. "Mitzie Point" is the old "Jackson Hill."

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: [Footnote] It was called "IV Hill" because the two valleys on the face of the hill look like the letters "I" and "V" from Corvallis (from the south). the valleys also looked like "dimples."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Key or Smith Hill, Poison Oak Hill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know anything about it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know Forest Peak?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So those hills two ridges back you're not familiar with?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did. . when you went to Sulphur Springs on your horse, did you take a route from your family

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: farm across some right of ways and you took the old grade on Lewisburg Saddle, do you recall any parts of that old grade that are still visible?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The original route over the hill as I hear has been changed. And I hadn't been over it in a long time. See, I can't drive anymore and hadn't any horse. So, I'm dehorsed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about routes to the coast? Would you go along the hills towards Philomath or would you follow pretty much the same route that's there now or would you go over William Hill f you were going to Philomath?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm trying to think. Pretty much like it is now, but I don't remember exactly. Well, it's pretty much like it is now. I've been out there on horse.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] South of Philomath Out of Beaver Creek. Oh, okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The dahlia farm out there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There was a dahlia farm, it's not anymore is it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. Mrs. Vida R. Bullis is running it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long has it been a dahlia farm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Jimmy, must be twenty years or better.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that route would be pretty much where Highway 20 is now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know it by it's numbers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have a name for that road then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was just Beaver Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Beaver Creek Road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: From your place, was there a name for the road over to Beaver Creek Road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, Highland Way as far as it went, but you see that's on the southwest corner of town and town didn't come out so far in those days.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you'd take Highland Road into town and then from town you 'd go out to Beaver Creek Road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember the name of the road from town to Beaver Creek Road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the Philomath Highway.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Philomath Highway, okay. And the college was out there. Was Philomath quite a bit different In those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was smaller and the Corvallis wasn't nearly as wide.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you could say pretty much rural farm countiy?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, you know when my grandfather [Crees] was farming his two hundred acres it was in the middle of Corvallis [Today's Corvallis]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When he was farming it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And he quit farming in . . . he began fanning in '71.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Eighteen seventy-one?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was. . . do you know who's donation land claim he was on?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think he took it up, no, I don't know the name of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long did he farm that land?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, until after. . . about the turn of the century and he moved to town just before the turn of the century and retired.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know what crops he raised?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was all level then, so I imagine he raised an awful lot of wheat. There's a while there where Oregon just raised wheat until it wore the ground out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: All the farmers raised wheat?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've heard that it depleted the soil because they raised so much.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know when that started happening, when the soil started getting worn out?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, when . . . about the '70's because my other grandpa came here in '74 and he found it completely depleted.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So maybe from the 1850's to the 1870's, about twenty years in there they just wore the soil out?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then. . . what crop did they change to after they quit raising wheat?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. I know my father began raising rye grass for hay.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you raise that on.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And grandpa raised. . his hay was Timothy. .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So rye grass and Timothy would grow in poorer soil than the wheat?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they deplete the soil with that after awhile or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they didn't seem to have, they rotated more. Different field.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any of the amounts that they used to get off the wheat, how many bushels an acre or some . . . how did they know they were depleting the soil? Could the weather have been changing for bad for a couple of years and they got excited and blamed it on the soil?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so, no. Because when grandpa [Gragg] came he rented a farm down by Amity, near his daughter, she'd come in '64. And he had very bad luck, very poor crops, so he rented a different farm and it was the same thing. He tried three of them and the same thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Worn out?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Worn out. So then he went to Clatsop County and took up a donation land claim and it was covered with big trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Timber and Stone Act or something like that? Would that have been about 1890 that he did that or 1895?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Before that. . . . Oh, '78.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When he went to Clatsop County?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then did he log that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, he was too old, he retired.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Retired among the trees?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. No, they went out, you see, he was way back in and it was an awful job to get there and he and grandma went to a little town where they would have more conveniences. Little town of Mayer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kinds of crops did your father raise? I think you told me.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, he raised hay and he raised some wheats, and oats in the fields that way. Then he put

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: in the first walnut orchard in this area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember what year, about?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I was in high school, that was before 1914.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are any of those walnuts still there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where are they?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: On the old farm home.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So those walnuts they were put in about eighty years ago?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. And they're kind of sad because nobody does anything for them anymore.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who owns them now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Floyd. . what's his name . . . Anderson, Floyd Anderson, used to be the assessor.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would could be done to them to help them out?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they should have been pruned and taken care of somewhat as they go along or they're pretty sad. Then after. . . you see, he got the English walnuts and planted them and then when they began to bear he found out that he had a poor variety. That they got the early frost . . . late frost. So he bad to graft them to a more hardy strain and the next thing he did, he took walnut from the old walnut tree and raised seedlings and planted them and then grafted them to the English. And that's all there, but it has no care.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that's the first walnut orchard in the area, so it's got some significance as far as local crops?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you 'd like to see them fixed up and maintained?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, he had the place just tip top. Never been taken care of since he died.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are you familiar with other orchards in the area, or plantings or.. were there apple orchards, that you can remember when you were a kid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, yes. All the farms had an apple orchard, that old orchard that's there now is over a hundred years old.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know who planted it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. Some pioneer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Which apple orchard are you talking about?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: On my father's place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So when your father got it, it already had an old apple orchard on it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, and he pruned it up and got the dead limbs out and all that and then he sprayed it for. at that time the coddling moth had been around and laid her eggs and ever apple had a worm, so he had to spray for that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did he spray on them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The spray had sulphur in it, I don't know what it was called, but I do know that it had sulphur, you could smell it. There was an awful lot of work to farming by that time. An awful lot of vermits and insects and all kinds of things.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think there's the same vermits and insects in the 1870's when they were raising wheat?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't think so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think they came in because of the crops or. . . ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, telling why, they just. . . they just getting around then by that time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any in particular. . . you said coddling moths, was that something just came in one or two years..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they came in to stay, they're still here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know when they first came in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know whether they came in my grandfather's era or not, they sure were in Papa's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about other insects or maybe small animals or birds?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the animal that was the most destructive to crops was moles and gophers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there more gophers then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. My father had a line of traps out most of the time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So gopher trapping was kind of one of the chores for subsistence farming?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What other kind of animal control., would you have problems with skunks in the hen house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, you would if you left the door open at night; they shut the door.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about coyotes or raccoons?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, didn't see either one of them. They came in later.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Coyotes and raccoons?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did they come from?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But they weren't around this area, after awhile they started coming in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think maybe. .there may have been some in the hills, have you heard, but you know this winter I've heard coyotes yelling.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This winter?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Over that way somewhere, some faintly.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about black bears?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no bears.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I was cutting timber on Misty Point and a black bear chewed on my chain saws just a few years ago. Three years ago they were right next to the valley. How about deer, has the deer population.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: .got larger or smaller?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I don't know, but.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember different kinds of deer, were there any white tailed deer here then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember of it, of course at first I was too little to pay attention. I know my father didn't hunt much. He'd get a grouse once in awhile and during China pheasant season. They used to be thick. Then somebody brought in fox and he went to work and reproduced and they ruined the Chinese by getting their nests on the ground.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there 's foxes in here now that are wild?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was for awhile, I don't know if they're still there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And those are what you think killed off the ph.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, you see the pheasants' nest is on the ground, just duck soup to the foxes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why did people bring in foxes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They didn't have any more sense.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just. . for hunting or for pets.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: . I don't know why, but it was ridiculous to bring it into this area where it was getting more settled all the time and agricultural.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So somebody somewhere brought in foxes and for awhile there's a lot of them, do you remember about when that was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it was after I was grown, I know that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it was a scandal type thing?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Everybody's got pheasant hunting and suddenly everybody's got foxes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did they control the foxes, what did they do with them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. I imagine some of the farmers shot them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about opossum?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They came later, and I've had my times with them. They're very persistent and they got under my house and I had a whale of a time getting them Out. I finally douched them out and into a big cage thing and then I used my little pistol on them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just killed them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's the only thing to do.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You don 't like opossums?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, they're too destructive. Eat everything and chew things. Very great nuisance.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember when they came into this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I had my troubles after I came here and that's oh, twenty years ago.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, were they here in the 1920's?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not that I know of.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you didn't notice them really until about twenty years ago?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't have anything have any dealings with them then, you see, I wasn't. . . I was on the farm then and if there were any opossums around I didn't ever see them. Of course, we had dogs and the dogs would have scared the opossums.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about beaver, were there beavers on any of these streams through here, beaver ponds -- were they common?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't remember of it, they're such little streams. I don't remember of it. Some of my friends in Alsea had beaver trouble and a few others have, but I never did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about did your father fish or are you familiar with fish in the streams around here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, there were trout, my brother and I fish, but there wasn't much for a grown up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just small fish?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, small trout, we thought it was fun.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were you fishing Oak Creek, or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, the streams on his place, a little .two little streams.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they have names?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I named them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Two little. . . what did you name them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, one, the land it flowed through was kind of clay and gooey and I called it. . . what was it called now, it had to do with the ground, and the other on the north end was different soil and stuff and there are lots of periwinkles, so I called it Periwinkle Creek. Cave In, this one in this end kept caving in, kept washing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are they still there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are they still called.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what they're called. I don't know what they're called anymore.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] Across from the high school.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So do you think they still have fish in them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They wouldn't have much, but they might have a few in them, I doubt if they're. . we had some nine or ten inches when we're kids.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Those are worth. . .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. We thought it was wonderful.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you notice many -- were there more ducks or geese in those days, wild ducks and geese?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There were . . . yes, flying over, but they didn't land here. But I saw enormous bands of geese migrating, you know, and then for the last few years you don't see hardly any or hear them. I heard some this winter, but they're not big bands like they used to be.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When did that start changing, do you remember?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I wasn't looking. I don't know just when they was -- just came to my attention and now it's just recent years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the way that the changes have come from wheat to hay, when they went to that what did they use for the taxes, how did they generate money to pay the taxes on these small fanns?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they fed the hay to the cows and milked the cows.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it was milk, that's what a lot of farmers used for their income was milk, they were dairy fanns?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Part of it, you see, they had a variety, a farmer just can't depend on one thing unless it's big.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Apples and eggs and hogs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, a little bit of everything.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did people raise sheep?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Papa had some sheep. Sheep and cattle and horses, goats.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any of the other apple orchards, were there quite a ftw apple orchards, are there any cherry orchards in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We had a cherry orchard and made some money selling that too. I don't remember whether big orchards, they all had orchards when I was a child, but I don't know whether they were removed or what. I don't get out among them where the old neighbors used to live.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would there be pickers, like would Siletz Indians come across to pick or kids pick?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, neighbor kids mostly, and me and my brother.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, mostly the kids of the farms that did that the harvesting.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were there to work.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there any hired hands to help out?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, Papa always had a hired hand, he had too much to work by himself. I helped him out a little bit in . . . when he was planting crops, I would drive a three horse team to the rake, harrow I mean. To cover the grain after he sowed it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would that be sowed by machine or hand?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He usually sowed it by hand, but he had a little hand machine with some of the grains he would sow with that I remember, but I think most of it he threw it by hand. I noticed he had a sack on his left side and he'd throw this and bring his hand back and get another handful, he had a system you see.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He had a rhythm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And he had me rake, I mean harrow over to cover the grain because sometime there'd be a big flock of blackbirds or crows would descend and pick it up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How would you keep them out of there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, you don't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You just have to let nature have.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, if you rake. . . harrow it over.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, Isee.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: with the birds, you cover it up, they wouldn't get much of it. I've done all the different things on the farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why do you think there's not so many farms anymore?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I don't know why for sure, but I think it's too bad.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: . . too many people? . Well, I imagine there are several reasons all put together.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You think it would be nice f.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It would be a whole lot better than hordes of people on charity.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, do you think it would be worth it to even have a couple family farms just so kids would know what family farms look like?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, and some sort supervision and teaching. (end of tape 1)

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: An old Indian camp?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, that's what we were told, and I have found broken pieces of Indian stone bowls.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: In that area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. On my dad's farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What part of the farm were those broken bowls on?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: As I remember it was in a field, but I'm not sure now. But I've got them out in my museum. No, I don't remember. He would mainly he would dig them up with his farm tools, you see, and bring them in, because there are marks on some of them where he's hit them with his machine.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, they were excavated on his farm just where he had the fields and you 're not too sure where exactly.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, somewhere on the farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Have you heard any stories about that village or what they may have done there or just.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no. Nobody seemed to know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just that Indians used to live there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any other sites around here where you were told Indians used to live?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I think I have but I don't remember now where it was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember finding any arrowheads or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, yes, I have found a few arrowheads.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall where? Do you recall where the arrowheads were?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, no, it's liable to be most anywhere on the farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, on the farm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah, just on the farm, but I didn't remember a particular place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are they in your museum too?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, and so you found those in the early 1900's?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is says here, too, that your father came up with your Gragg grandparents, is that how it was spelled or was it Gragg?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: (Gragg), Scotch.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the old Ajax ship, and then she doesn 't say what the old Ajax ship is, do you know what that is?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it was from San Francisco. My grandfather came by train to San Francisco when they moved in '78. . . '74.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did he come from?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Missouri.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: By railroad to San Francisco?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. And then they came up the coast to Astoria on the old Ajax, which later sunk.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so that was the name of the boat?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, the A/ax?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did it sink?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: On the west coast here somewhere, I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then from Astoria they moved down into this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, no, they moved into a little, . . oh, first they went to Amity where my aunt lived who had come ten years before.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they went there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was she from Missouri?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there a reason she came right after the Civil War?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the reason?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, a bunch of them were coming, a bunch of her relatives, her family and some of her relatives and neighbors and they came in a wagon trail with oxen.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oxen wagon trail?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they come by the south route or the north route?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Don't ask me, I wasn't there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Nobody told you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I wished I had known about those things. I would have asked her when I could.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: She was still alive when you were young?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. My aunt Sophronia.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Sophronia. So you actually knew somebody that came across the Oregon trail by covered wagon?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. And I've known others too but I can't remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was she the first one of your relatives that came here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The first one that came. And when she came and her family, grandpa wanted to come, but grandma wouldn't. So ten years later the grasshoppers ate them out in. . . oh, Kansas not Missouri, Kansas. The grasshoppers ate them out and grandma was willing to come then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Had her fill of grasshoppers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Just mined them, had them two years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did she ever regret it? Did she like it out here when they came here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now that was your father's family, right.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then how did your mother's family come here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Grandpa caine. . . oh, Pennsylvania is where they lived. Mama was born in Pennsylvania. And they came out here in. . goodness sakes, I can't think of the year. She was born back . there in . . . oh, it was '71.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. He came to this farm that was surrounded by town later.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So even when he was still farming the town grew up all the way around him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wasn't he under pressure to develop ii' or sell it for money?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. He didn't sell it money.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did people offer to buy it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, he didn't want to sell it. He rented it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] Is that the one down on Grant?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. And then you see,

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] With the Crees house.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. That big old house is still living, but it isn't white anymore. Painted it an icky color.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You'd like to see it white again?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. And I'd like to see it have a decent setting, it's crowded in among houses.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you think it should be moved?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's been moved, you see.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In recent years a man bought it I suppose for speculation and he moved it to a place where it isn't fit for it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It's out of context?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] Where was it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Sixteenth and. . what's the other street? .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they moved it into a bad location and painted it an icky color?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Maybe because of it's age, maybe sometime in the future somebody can move and restore it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I wish somebody could.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] Is that picture she's got on the wall in there, is that down on sixteenth?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Will you go get that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's one thing I want to ask you later on is do you have good photographs of the early days of the farms or of the local hills or your family in the early 1900's or late 1800's?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Some, just some. I'll hunt it up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What I'm curious, is sometime at some later date would it be possible to borrow those and take photographs of them for slides?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Are they all pretty much in a single location or scattered around pretty much?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] This is it when it was on sirteenth. Picture of the Cree house.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Crees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Crees house and "God Bless Our House" sign was on Sixteenth, do you know what year this is, it doesn't have a. . . oh, wait. . . no it doesn't have a year. It was printed in Portland. 1878.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] I'm tiying to figure out what those hills are, that's Timber Hill and that's IV Hill behind it, there 's the ridge up in Dunn Forest. There's an orchard there and fir starling to move in here, fir back up in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] But most of Vinyard Hill was pretty bare. And so you made this her letterhead.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My kids think it's great.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So do I.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now you see, my father's farm is in these hills back of the bani to the right up Highland Way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this is your Grandfather Crees and this is Highland Way up here and this would be your father's farm up through here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] Kind of over by. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Over the hills, over the hills.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's why we're not seeing any trees in that area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, that's trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But just up on the ridge there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that mostly oak?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they young oak.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A fir or two.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they younger trees or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Quite a bit younger.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This is beautiful. What I'd like to do with this at sometime is take a slide picture so it can be projected on a screen and enlarged, would that be possible?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I should think so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: If. . . is there. . . I understand there's somebody that's working with you now doing a story of your lfe and working on a histoty?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I'm not sure what it is, I haven't read it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, you trust that's what she's doing?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would she be a good person to maybe help you gather some of your old photographs together?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Because f you could put them together it would be worth keeping a permanent record, maybe one that the Homer Museum or Oregon State could have access to. . . to see how things have changed in time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Give me some time to hunt them up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Well, f you're willing to do it, I would sure be willing to take the photographs and make duplicates for you.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'll see if I want them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Any pictures of your family and grandparents are just as interesting as farms or old buildings or early Corvallis.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Might be.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And she might be a good person to gauge which pictures are.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, no doubt. Now that's grandpa's orchard.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that's one that he inherited . . . or he planted that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is this the walnut orchard we were talking about?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no, this is grandpa Crees'.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And he planted that orchard?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are any of those trees still standing?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm not sure. There's one stood for a long, long time but that was a Belflower Apple.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Belflower Apple?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was an old timer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And it still might be there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And it was planted?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, he. . .whenever he planted it, I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] You say that was down on Sixteenth and what was the cross street.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm trying to think of it, but I don't remember the cross street. Yeah, I may have it written down here, but . . Well, yes he came there in '71, you see and he stayed until '78.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so this picture says 1878 on the background because these trees are older than six or seven years old. So this picture might be from 1890 or 1900.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I'm not sure.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It's a nice picture. It would be nice if somebody bought the house and moved it back and painted it that color again. Is that one of the oldest homes still around here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, no.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's quite a few older homes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Some of them have renovated and preserved.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Other than riding your horse, did you play with other kids?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes, but you see it's quite a ways between houses and not all houses people had children to play with. But there was one in particular and it was down on Highland Way down this way down the hill And that was quite a little ways to walk, of course, I'd go on my pony if I went but they had to walk. They did come out to the cherry orchard. And they're the ones that gave me my first start of botany.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The girls in that family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many were there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Ten.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ten girls?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, ten children.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see. And one or two of them were interested in botany?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. Several of them. Kings.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, the Kings. Soloman Kings 'family.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: His grandchildren.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did they get interested in botany?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, well, they had to make their own fun, most everybody did on the ranch. And they were great on reading books like Little Women, Little Men, Little Women and all those nice books of the times. And they got started on it and they made up their own names for them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: For the plants?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they started identifying the plants?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You bet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And giving them. . . kind of like your naming creeks, and them naming plants?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. They were just wonderful. And the oldest one lived to be ninety-eight.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, did they drink some of that water at Sulphur Springs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well that's., we might have a competitor for Pepsi Cola here pretty quick. When you got together with them did you play games like hide and seek or race horses or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we never. . . not much like that, but the neighbors on the right of my father's place were the Murphys, a fellow related to my husband, just a cousin though. And they had a bunch of kids and they were my age and we would certainly play. In the evenings, lots of times we'd go over there into their barn lot and play their base and all those rough games. One time a little red headed boy, Roy and I collided and I had a black eye for a long time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just from rough housing?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Running, you know, we'd get so excited about the games.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, would you build tree houses or play catch with a baseball or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, a little later when my brother got old enough to play ball, we did a lot of that, but we never made any tree houses. But we climbed trees to beat the band especially the shorter trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So tree climbing and tag and rough housing and horse back riding those were. . .fishing, those were the things. . . and reading?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any of the books you used to read?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. I used to get books out of the library and Mama and Papa and I took turns reading them out loud in the evening.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember some of those books?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes and no. There were popular books of the day, popular authors, and I can't say them. I should write that down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You could probably look it up too.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Little Men and Little Women were two of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's Alcott?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you go to movies or baseball games?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wasn't any.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No reason to go to town?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes, we had to go to take our produce in and buy what we couldn't raise. See every week we took milk and eggs or they'd perish and we had to drive the old black horse to the. surrey with a fringe on top.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was your produce wagon then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so about just once a week you'd go into town, until you started school?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Everything was different then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You think a lot nicer?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I do.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think people were nicer as a result or. ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, in general I guess not.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Same kind of people just nicer circumstances?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Some I read about are not nice. Some are very queer to me.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The way things are going?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. I wonder why. One thing that they had to work and be sensible in those days. And there's too much leisure and pleasure now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you think what you did as recreation as a kid is just about the right amount, and now they do it too much?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think that. . . like welfare or something like that, or do you think it's just absence of family farms or just a bunch of reasons?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A bunch of reasons. Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that something in the last ten years or something since World War II, or. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, in the last quite a few years but it's getting worse. It really is. Now there's poverty in my day too. There were certain families that never got anywhere, but they travelled

entries.speaker: editorial
