entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where would you go, did you have fireworks?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We had them in the evening, throwing firecrackers. . . yes . . .the kids were always using firecrackers all day long.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the Fourth?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would there be some community celebration around here somewhere?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Lots of times, yes. That's. . .1 don't know, I don't think they went to Sulphur Springs particularly. It was just on some place here in the area where there was room.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And they might have a fireworks display or something?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would your family. . . was it common for families to go picnicking.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: . on their own farms or would they go down by the river

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, no, on their own farms and several. . . . some of their friends from other areas. communities might come or something like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about when they were gathering crops and stuff, would they take meals out to the fields and maybe have a family picnics or hired hands. . . set a place.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no, come to the house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Come to the house and eat there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, more comfortable.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they were looking for comfort rather than.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they worked hard and had a meal and washed up and rested up a little.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long did you work at the seed.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just about fifteen years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you would have been forty or fifty years old when you quit working there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I worked until I was sixty-two. . . maybe it was sixty-five, I'm not sure.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then you retired?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And since that time, you've been devoting most of your time to botanizing or a little bit of your time or ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. I have a variety. Like him and some of the others we got together about it and call ourselves the "Botany Gang".

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Botany Gang, huh?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Botany Bunch, I guess isn't it?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When did this happen?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, several years ago, do you remember?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it's like the Brady Bunch8 or something?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Got thirty-two years there? What did you do between your retirement and the Botany Bunch?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I was always busy .. an old hen with a dozen chickens.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Volunteer work or grandkids or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, stuff I cooked up myself. Before I moved here, I had a garden and I gardened. But I've been working at my yard here, to get it ready to plant in wild flowers and save some of them maybe. I fmished that job this spring.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: [Footnote] Brady Bunch was a popular television show in 1970s.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you're going to put the lawn into wildflowers rather than grass?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm not going to try for grass.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Trying to keep it out?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it'll be wild flowers, I've got twenty kinds now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Twenty kinds?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are they fairly common around the area or some of them unusual?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, fairly common. You know what the trilliums are, don't you?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I've got trifliums and I've got. . . well, it's that one. . . lamb's tongues {Erythronium oregonum].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Lamb tongue?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, been seeing it here, well, that's what I wanted.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you collect wild plants when you were working at the Seed Lab?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I went with my teacher on a few collecting trips. There, oh, here. See they're like that in my yard now, in the spring.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. Did you ever go botanizing on Coffin Butte, that area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, that's down that way isn't it?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I used to see it, we used to drive by it but I've never got to go up on it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about. . .1 understand that you've identified plants in the area of the Soap Creek School House?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, they have a yard there and it's full of cat's ears [Calochortus tohniei].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Cat ears?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Mariposa Lilies, local kind. And they have a committee to take care of that school house, you know it's a museum. And the one who's supposed to take care of the yard didn't. she's a Japanese girl and she didn't understand what to do, so she mowed it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And they're trying to raise wildflowers there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it was just thick with them and you see, that takes all the seed pods and no more seeds and the bulbs will run out eventually. So they had to stop that and had her just mow a path.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So now they're not mowing it to encourage the wildflowers to come back?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that discouraged it, see, that took the seed pods.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is there still a fairly good variety of wildflowers there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it just this kind, the cat ear.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They were saying that recently they found a fairly rare lily towards the back of the house? Are you familiar with that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I hadn't heard about that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just about two days..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's interesting. I would like to know what kind of lily.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's why I was asking you.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, you have to show me.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, we'll go find it. Lorna Grabe.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] She '11 stand right there and say, well, that's not supposed to be there. I think Lorna Grabe 's the one you want to talk to, she's the one that told me about it, she said they just found it. . . I believe within the last year.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I know her, I'll have to call her and ask her.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: In the notes here, in those days, there were lots ofjack rabbits?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, my, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was a real problem around here, jack rabbits?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I don't know how much of a problem they were, for awhile they were quite thick. I don't know what happened to them. Sometimes they'd get a disease among rabbits or some other animal and it takes them off.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So in those days there were more gophers, more moles and more jack rabbits here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think all this asphalt that we're laying down is what's helping to control them or do you think it's just that they 're not farming any more or do you think diseases maybe came in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Any of those can help, any of those can be part reason, you see. Various things, no doubt. But there's plenty of moles, I don't know about gophers, but I . . . as I go along the road I see in the field piles of mole and gopher works. There's still plenty of them around.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It not so much a problem maybe because people aren't farming?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's right. You don't want them on your lawn, sometimes they're on your lawn.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they're still a problem some?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes, they can be a problem.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the way the town's been developing, you got to watch it develop from dirt roads to concrete parking lots?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Dirt roads to gravel roads to concrete.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think maybe they've put too much concrete down or do you think that's just one of the prices you pay for having so many people?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes, you have to have it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about this plan to have a green way plan around the city, do you think something like that is a pretty reasonable idea or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, probably so, I haven't looked into it, I don't know what. . . don't know much about it yet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think it might be better off to turn it into family farms?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the county all around has good land, now all this land over here that Camp Adair ruined. That could have just as well been made into farms.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The flat area, the area around where Wells Station is.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I've been seeing in the paper about the Camp Adair.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They said some of that land was ruined because of all the concrete and pipes of excavation.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, probably so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you think that their using it for a game farm, do you think it might be better to raise pheasants there or put in a few family farms maybe as demonstrations?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. If it's got trash in it like cement and the pipes and things, they couldn't do much about fanning it. Perhaps it's best this way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember when CCC came in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that pretty popular with the people in your area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we just stood for it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just happened so you lived with it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they create any problems?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not where I was, but. . .1 don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know any people that maybe came here with the CCC and that are still here, liked the area so much they stayed?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't particularly a person, no.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was just kind of one of those troublesome things that kind of occurred and didn't pay it any mind?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about Adair? Was that kind of the same reaction or did people. . . were people more concerned when Adair came in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't hear much about it. I guess it was the same way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, even though they had these big development out around Peavy and Camp Adair, they kind of kept to themselves and didn 't attract a lot of people here locally or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Maybe they had more a tendency to go up to Portland or Salem when they went places than Corvallis or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Probably.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Could it have been that you were just maybe. . . because of your kind of work or lifestyle that you just weren't too much associated with any changes around town?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I guess that's it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: As far as you were concerned, you knew what was going on but didn't really change things too much?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about either one of the Wars in general, World War I, can you remember any big changes because of that, a lot less men around or lot of community fundraisers for.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, there was some of that, but I. . in general it didn't upset our. . . or disrupt our lives . much. Got along. . got life here fairly well.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have any close relatives die or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. I lost two cousins in one family.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, that was the worst thing?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Some of the boys would go off to war and not come back?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there any local celebration after the War, or was there a lot of.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, yes there was. I think there was. Everybody celebrating.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the Depression. Was that a real sudden thing that upset everybody or poor family farms anyhow and the people kept on as usual?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, well, about as usual, I suppose affected some more than others.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Businesses in town, did some of the businesses close down or. . . not paying them for awhile or. sell out?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I imagine so, but I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So life was pretty stable, wars had come, depressions would come, CCC came in and as far as you went just something you read in the newspaper?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. See, the farm . . . I don't know how to say it, but it can absorb a lot of trouble and bother and one thing or another.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Pretty insulated about world events . . . or even local events?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. You had your work to do and you had to do in order to live.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you listen to the radio much?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, can't be bothered.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, do you think you're unusual or do you think that was maybe a lot of people?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Most people.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Didn't listen to the radio?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they like it, but I haven't got the habit.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I rather read a good book.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, maybe a lot. [END OF TAPE]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Did you talk to her and know that they used to live in Soap Creek Valley?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. You knew Neva?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I knew the whole family, but Neva was in my grade.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you went to the same school?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, but that's after they moved to town you see.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see, so do you remember when they moved to town?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, it was around the turn of the century.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About 1900 or 1901?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see, so you knew them, the Moores, in town and went to school with them and the Kings?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they ever talk or go back to the old place on Sulphur Springs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. Laura [Moore] has lived the longest I believe and she corresponds with the people that are taking care of the little red school house. She helps them with memories.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And I've got some photographs of her but I haven't talked to her. Do you think she would be a good person to talk to about. . . as far as. . . or was she too young when they moved to remember much about Sulphur Springs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, because she is older than me.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see and she's still alive?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She was just a few years ago.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And she had a good memory two years ago too?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I may. . . did she move to Newport?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think so. At the coast.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And one of her sisters was still alive, I think, maybe in Philomath? I'm not really.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was Laura and Neva and there was a boy or two. Mr. Moore had, in Corvallis, had a chicken hatchery. Oh, I see so That was his business.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Sold the ranch and moved to town and opened up a chicken hatchery. Were they. . . did they do pretty good?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. It was considered pretty good.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They lived in a house in town then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. They were living there when I started to school in 1901 or '02, whatever it was and Neva was in my grade. Integrated school, there was no grades in this country school.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, did you like the school in town better or the country school better?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I didn't go to the country school hardly two years. It was a better school in town, of course, I've got to admit that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Got to ride your horse.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have a May pole or any /dnd of playground equipment, any slides or merry go round?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, they had slides and things like that in town. Nothing out in the country one. We'd play just games we knew like Drop the Handkerchief and Pussy Wants a Corner and things

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think you got a pretty good education in the schools?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes, they were good.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Got reading and writing of course, how about Oregon history, did they teach much histoty?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, and I like history.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, did they teach local history about Jessie Apple gate or Jedidiah Smith or can you remember?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I'm not sure, I've heard of them before so . . . I don't remember whether there was much of that mentioned or not.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Still a lot of pioneers alive at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they make a big deal out of them, did they have local celebrations for the original pioneers or

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't remember any of it. And it was 1905 before they began to urge to mark the Oregon Trail.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember the man responsible for that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, Ezra Meeker.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you know him personally?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I saw him personally.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Saw him, so he was a big hit when he was marking the Oregon Trail?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, he had to work hard at getting people interested.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He's kind of famous. I'm interested in trails and he 's kind of a.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You see in 1905 when the Lewis and Clark Exposition.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you go to that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, in Portland.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have Coca Cola there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. I don't think so. Anyway Ezra . . . we stayed at my aunt in Portland for a few days, we went and Ezra was camped with his oxen team and wagon on a vacant lot near her. And he was on his way back east to Washington to work for getting the trail marked.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was he part of the exposition?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no. Just happened to be there, or maybe he did on it on purpose, I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you talk to him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so, I was just a kid, but I saw him and I heard him talk a little.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] He went back East by wagon?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Took him a long time, but he finally got back to Washington D. C.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was he famous then, did people know who he was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, he began being famous, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you take the train to the Lewis and Clark Exposition?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think we did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What do you remember about it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh boy, plenty. The main thing that interested me was that pony that had been taught tricks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Trick pony?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Trixie.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember the log house. . the world's largest log cabin? Can you remember the big log cabin they built there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes, yes, I saw it, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What other impressions, is that the first you can remember going to Portland?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, because we'd go there and visit my grandmother and my aunt every so often.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember anything about Portland in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it wasn't as big as now of course. You could go on the train there. No, I can't remember much detail.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Could you take a boat there, did they still have boats.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, we could have done that but it's a lot slower, you know and all that than the train.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It wasn't as modem? Would people still take the boat?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know how much it was used. I think it was more for freight than passengers at that time. But when my mother and I caine to Benton County from Clatsop County, I think. was it Portland, I can't remember, to visit somebody, we took the boat to Corvallis, the river boat. And I can't remember where it was a stern wheeler or a side wheeler. I wish to goodness I did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you remember taking the boat ride?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I remember.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] Other than you and your mother, were there very many passengers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it was passengers like us, you know, just passengers. Coming up here. . . See we was coming up here because we were moving up here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Moving your freight up that way?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not all of it. My dad came across the mountains. . Elsie where he lived with a wagon and horses and a herd of cattle. And he hit the road coming up . . . but he was supposed to come across part of the Military Road with that and he hit the road. . . the main road down here somewhere I think around Amity maybe. . . and it took him many days to get up here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So your family was here waiting for him when he got here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we didn't get here until after he had been here a few. . some days.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did he come by himself?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, he had two or three neighbors, he hired them. . . to help him come with his cattle and things. And he had to get. . . buy food. Oats and stuff for them along the way, and he found some people who weren't very accommodating.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What do you mean by that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they didn't want to sell him anything, this and that and the other. . . I don't know what all. It was one in particular I think, became our neighbor later on. Wasn't much accommodation between us.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Hard feelings on the road translated to hard feeling between neighbors?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: See

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I thought you were starting to say something and I.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, but I've. . . then you see, I've seen my whole life from then on and what he did to this ranch . . . that old ranch and I'd say it would be a whole lot better if a lot of people now that are at loose ends and don't know what to do with themselves and can't get anywhere if they had a little farm they could work out. But they'd have to be taught something.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: People don't have the knowledge or the tools to work on the farms anymore?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no! And. . . especially if you could fmd a boy that's out of high school or has quit high school or something, he's the one that needs help. Nothing's done.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the children 's farm home here locally, do you think something like that. . is that what . you have in mind?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I. . well, anything to get them started, yes. I don't know how . . . I remember when . the farm home was started, but I've never gone over there and seen how it works.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just not interested or just didn't have the opportunity?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just didn't seem to have the opportunity. I always was busy.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On your father, when he moved into the farm, the soil had been depleted and it had been used for stock, is that common with a lot of the farms around here if they 'ye been depleted, they just switched over to stock?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, or if they .. I don't know why they left it, anyway it's gone back to nature. And it's very, very interesting.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: In what ways?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: For instance, there were two natural springs on the place, wonderful springs, that's where we got our water, one at both ends of the place and when papa fmally got himself a little time to fix up another field, way down to the north end, I remember we all went down there with him that day and around that spring had grown up young ash trees, they were probably as high as this house then and in every one of those ash trees as near as I remember there was a nest that looked like a robin's nest. And there was a . . . I think was a deer mouse. Do you know anything about deer mice? They're pretty grey with a white belly and a long tail. And there was that mouse, I don't know what it was doing there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Every one of those nests?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. And when we went down there, and began to chop them trees, of course, they'd beat it. We ruined their environment and I feel bad about it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think the deer mice had more right to those trees than you did?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it's a shame really. They weren't doing any harm and we were ogres to them. And.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] Are you sure it was a deer mouse or could it be something like tree voles?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now what's a tree

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] Looks like a mouse, there are a bunch of them and live . . . they make nests in trees.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it could have been, you see, I didn't know. Nobody knew to tell me. I'd like to know because I want to write this up about my father's place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you're working on a history of your father's making that transformation?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. And things that happened as they appeared to me and. . . at all ages as I grew up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] You say they were grey with a white belly?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Have you noticed, when you were younger can you recall seeing eagles or more hawks?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. Hawks, more hawks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: More than now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about owls?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, there were more owls too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And lots more pheasants?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. You see the pheasants were brought in about the '90's. And they prospered and they got too thick, I'll say, for years. And now, they're just about gone.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I hunted pheasants around here in the 1950's and the '60's even, until 1960's, so it's been pretty recent that they've kind of died out.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Well, I don't see them, I know there's nothing like they used to be. Maybe some living yet, but nothing like it was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did the grass seed growers putting all these fallow farms back into production after World War II, could that have removed their habitat, been more problem than foxes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You think pretty much foxes was..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I think foxes were the big. . . a big factor in it. And then another little critter. I'd like to know somebody to ask that knows about these little critters. And this one as I remember was more like a field mouse, it was a little browner but it was about as big as a deer mouse and it had a short tail and it was a fat little thing, you know, shaped like a mole or a gopher but it was a mouse and it lived in this . . . swamp . . . this brush grass swamp.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that's the place you saw it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. And the only place it could dig and do anything about living would be in the clumps of roots. I'd like to talk to somebody that would know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think I could probably find out for you.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I wish you would.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've got a friend that's a wildlife biologist.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, goodie.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can probably help you out.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would like to talk to somebody, about both those kinds of mice.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And another thing about this swamp, I will never forget it, it was below the run off of the spring and always had water, as I remember it never went dry completely and but it was very, very thin scum of water and real fme soft dirt and in the summer time when it was warm that water was wann. And boy was that the most wonderful place to run in bare feet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. What happened to it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I riled it up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No, I mean is it still there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, no, Papa. . . here's more Scotch thrift, he sunk a line of tile. . . that ruined that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he could plow over it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. I was interested in the aesthetic part of his farming. He was interested in profits.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it profitable to sink the tile and farm over that or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. It wasn't doing any good except for me otherwise.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see. How many brothers and sisters did you have?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, just one little brother.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How much younger than you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Six years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Six years younger?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Six or seven.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you were by yourself quite a bit?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, really.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So places that you would find and play with kind of by yourself and those are the areas that you became familiar with, places such as the spring, or the.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The creeks. Of course, he got big enough to play at the creek too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So those would be kind of your destinations around the house there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then the trees?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Shorter trees than that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. Oh, it was a heavenly place for kids if they were inclined that way. And I've got some real great granddaughters that aren't being taught a thing on earth about what grows. They're just little dolls, that's all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you know you were in a nice place when you were growing up or did it take your growing up and looking back to realize it was a nice place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I think both. Yeah, I realized it twice. As farms go, some people. . if anything I . don't like, it's a snob that makes fun of farms. But of course, farmers hung together, they were a social group and it was about the same, we didn't have any snobs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about when you went to college?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I didn't notice it, it was in a different environment. All in college and studying, didn't notice much like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think the courses they taught in college at that time were similar to courses they teach now, I mean, take away computers and some of the modem technology, were the instructors and students

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: was it a similar level of education or similar. Yes, I think so. environment. Yes. Of course, I enjoyed the botany the best of anything

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That wasn't your degree was it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I graduated in home economics, the thing I didn't care for. There wasn't much else for a woman to do then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The botany was that necessary for the job at the seed lab?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That helped like everything. I knew the names of things. I didn't have to ask.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you get more money because of that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't think so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just helped to ma/ce get the job?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes it would have, but they took lots of that didn't have any at all. They had to learn it there. Those were good days, I enjoyed the job.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Before then you were just . . . pretty much between graduation and starting at the Seed Lab, though you got married and were raising kids, pretty much as a housewife?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Oh, yes, I didn't have any job, of course I was busy. . we had a garden and all that sort of thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you do any botanizing during that time of your life?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. I always played with it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just go out and hike in the woods and look for things?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Where ever I was. I fmd there's something everywhere.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, even in your lawn or in the garden or..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. Constantly.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about your children?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they like it, but they didn't go in for it big like I did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where are some of your favorite places around town? You mentioned Sulphur Springs. Are there other areas that you think are particularly good for botanizing?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they're all good. Yes, I've been up on the face of these bare hills I didn't think about it then but I don't imagine, do you Phil, that there'd be a heck of a lot there, because it would just be hot and dry up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] . . . early in the spring why it's still. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you go more on the north side of the hills where it's cooler and moister looking for things?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I try to go on all different kinds of places, see, because different plants in different

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: places.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever map them or keep records?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Or journals or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just a good memory?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know how good it is, but I don't remember keeping much of a record.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are there any particular trails that you go on year after year to see certain plants at certain times?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, Sulphur Springs was the best, they're so different over there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, I know they 're thinking of developing it now and that's a good thing to know is that type of. that's locally a good area.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, it is, I think it ought to be preserved and done something with. It's different.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When was the last time you were out there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Two or three years ago, I think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'm trying to get Charlie Olson and Wanda Cook, it's the Cooks that bought the Moore place.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh. I didn't know any of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: She 's one of the Marc/cs..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And Charlie Olson up to Sulphur Springs in February and it maybe fun for you to go out at the same time, they're arguing over whether there was a building there or not, they don't know it yet. One says one thing and one says the other.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I can't remember. . . I think there was a building there when we first came. because this man Mr. Baker owned it and he made a croquet grounds.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Pennanent croquet?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: For the customers there and I think there was a building. . . it was just used for storage and temporary camping and things like that, nobody lived there that I know of. There were other people around the Valley, but nobody there that I remember of.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So would people pay money to play croquet it was like.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, he just had it for his guests.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did anybody pay him to stay there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He was just kind of a.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He owned it. just a nice guy and let everybody come and camp there that wanted to? Yeah, I don't know whether the campers had to pay .. those that camped in a tent. I don't know if they had to pay him when they were camped there overnight or anything.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, by the way there was a trail. . . Phil, maybe you know about this, we came in. went over west that way, we came in to the Sulphur Springs on a trail and I remember we'd come . . . several of us go horseback when Camp Athir was here and had built some tables and benches and things. And we'd come in on a trail.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: To Sulphur Springs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: From the southwest corner

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: From Oak Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you took. . . I think that trail is still there, from Oak Creek up and over to Sulphur Springs?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] Describe to me again where the trail came from?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, you see, I didn't pay much attention and some others in the group knew where to go and I just followed, but it came in somewhere from the southwest but I don't know where we got onto it or anything more about it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And it was during. . . when Camp Adair was there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, or after.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think I've got a map of that trail. I've got some maps of the trails in the 1930's in that area right up through 1945.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that. . . that must be it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, just go from Sulphur Springs head across the creek right across from where that little slab was, that concrete marker that says Sulphur Springs.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's where it came in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Close there. I don't know exactly.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember when that marker went in there, was it from.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I remember that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know when they put that there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not exact dates.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it Camp Adair or the CCC'S or was it there when you were a little girl?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it wasn't. It probably was the CCC's or some thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] Out there on the.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Can't think about where was I. Down there on Kings Road very likely is where I lived longest after I was married, and then when the girls got big enough, we got them . . . got another horse, you see.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] So that day you went on over the pass.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] You went back out west somewhere?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, we must have come from Kings Road. . I must have been living on Kings Road . then, and went on out Kings Road, I don't remember how we went, but we came out at Sulphur Springs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any old roads or trails that might have fallen down. . . California mines road or the Umpqua State Road or Applegate Trail or anything like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I've heard of the Applegate Trail.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you think it went through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did anybody tell you where?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, that's the trouble.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, but you did know. . . you did have an understanding that it came through here somewhere?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did anybody. . . can you remember anybody that might have told you that, one of the old timers that told you or. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, and they're all gone.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any of the people that said anything about it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think. . . one special one was my uncle, gave me that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Magnifying glass.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Goes everywhere with me.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, but he knew that the Applegate Trail came through?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, you see he was about my father's age, he knew a lot of these old time things.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he was interested in the local history here then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, because he grew up around. . . he grew up partly in Alsea and partly here. He knew a lot of people. Well, he was. . . gosh, he's been dead for. . . well, now, my husband died when my oldest child was seventeen, late was in the early twenties and I think Uncle gave me that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [Phil] Did he use that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, he used that lots, you see, he did some prospecting. He never made a strike.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Gold prospecting glass?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, he used it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any of the stories that he told other than mentioning the Applegate Trail, did he mention anything about Indians around here or mention any thing about Civil War days around here or anything of that nature?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't remember particularly, I wish I'd had sense enough to ask him. You see.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why don't we. . . we've put on. (end of tape)

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: [Interview conducted by Bob Zybach and Phil Hays at the home of Bessie Murphy, Valley View Drive, Corvallis.]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, I think we're recording Bessie, so why don't we start with why you are doing this.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let's see, how did I say it in the first place? I want to keep the history of this straight.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You were talking about the reason you were making your comments, why you thought this was important to get all the details in.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, I like history as it is. I don't want history distorted. So I may ask to make explanations so you'll understand what all this is. It isn't as it was as and it's different.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why is it important to you that we understand what it was like then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Did I say that?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Not yet.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, important is that I say that I want it right as it was. I don't want it distorted in the telling or anything. Because I can see it as it was, I knew it and I can see it as it was as I look back over my life.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You made some comments too about how it's important to you that people not make fun of farmers.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well I know that was a shortcoming of society. They had those who "had" plenty of this world's good and could have things as they want them, and they got the idea that they were a little better than those who didn't. And that isn't fair. We can't all be rich. We may just as worthy as anybody else. But it was the custom to make fun of something that was not quite as good as what you think you had. It just was that way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So people made fun of farmers back when you were a little girl too?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. If they could possibly get anything better they wouldn't live as next to nature as the farmers had to. But that don't make them any better. They thought it did, you see?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Did this show up when you were in grade school, between town kids and farmers kids?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, a little bit. But I didn't stick around after school long enough to hear many comments. I got on my pony and came home.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was Belle, wasn't it? No, that was.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Belle was your pony?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Doris was George's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So one thing I've found out about this. People can 't remember the names of their grandparents or their cousins but everybody knows the name of their pony and their work horses.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, you bet! A horse was very important to them in those days. Because it was its motive power on the farm until the tractors came in. And it's the inventions of labor saving devices that made the most change in the ways of life.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What's the biggest change you 'ye seen in your life?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Automobile from horses.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's what everybody says that's lived through that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You bet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] What were some other things chat came up on the farm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there were tractors, gasoline tractors, see that could push the horse out of reach.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You said. . . we were talking about Lady Bird Johnson putting all these wildflowers along the Texas highways. And you said it was important that people understand management.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. If they don't manage those plantings and keep them from being overpowered by the undesirable weeds, they won't have anything.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think it's good to use chemicals in management?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't think so. That will kill too many things. I don't know. I think that they will have to organize organizations and do a lot of hand weeding. That's my opinion. But they may figure out some other way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you think that putting these native plants back is good.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Urn hmm

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But the native plants.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They're a big price.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that's gonna be a lot of man power.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You bet. That's what I'm doing around here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now you also said that the farmers had to manage and had to pay attention, that they needed more respect, but one of the problems was, like with your own dad, that they got too focused. That they didn 'tpay attention to aesthetics.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, they lost track of some things that they shouldn't have. In the life. Because there was all the, there was the whole family to do something for. We didn't all just want to work our little heads off. We wanted to make a go of the farm and help him and all that, but that wasn't our sole interest. And my father's type, if you had time after you did all this work, you could do something about aesthetics. And I insist that they're important in the education.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now you also said what you thought was the worst mistake he made. Or the worst thing he did.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Not considerate enough.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You mentioned the one thing he did was what, draining that swamp?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, well, I suppose it was foolish of me to think that because that was good fanning. But oh, it spoiled it awful. Oh, that was a heavenly place, I tell you, for kids to play!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, was he being inconsiderate to you, or inconsiderate to the plants?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no, it was a necessity.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] That was part of why it was a poor farm, right, it hadn't been developed?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Or it had been allowed to go back to nature. It wasn't managed good. The springs, for instance, they were allowed to run and spread out and make swamps instead of being made into little streams to run off or something like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So on one hand there's a problem where you think we 'ye got to learn how to manage everything a lot better to take care of everybody, but on the other hand the price to pay is that we lose nature.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, that's right. Yes, you can't have everything.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What's the balance?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I haven't got a word for it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You think we need nature, but with so many people we've gotta maybe manage real intensely, to. 2

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I think so. I think you do have to.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That we just can't let nature take her course then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, because it takes too big a toll. And those swamps, I can't think of anything those swamps produce economically.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about wildflowers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well I mean that would have anything to do with the economy. A very very limited kind of spread of wildflowers because of the environment, it's too wet, only for just certain things. But, oh, but to wade in barefoot! Especially on a hot day! I can feel it yet! [Delighted laughter]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] How old were you when.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have an idea I was about 10 or 11.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] When they drained that swamp.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] So you had about five years to walk in it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, that was it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think we ought to have a certain amount of swamps, just for kids to play in? Maybe we can

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's the trouble, life's too luxurious.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Too expensive.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, it c not too fair that you got to play in them and that me and Phil don't get them.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I was two generations back, you see.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see. I guess you never got computers.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, you bet we didn't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, I think we covered the main points we wanted to cover in the general thing. We could maybe go back real briefly . . . we looked at the photographs and talked about your grandfather's wives. Maybe f you 'd like to talk a little bit about them, or were they in our previous conversation?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Just briefly.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Very briefly. I'd rather they be brief.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Because it was the only one that was bad, and I don't like to dwell on the bad any more than I have to.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, Phil made the point though, the comment about the Masons. I think that's a good one. Could you tell that story?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's record.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Could you talk about that a little bit then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, as I said, the Mason's got onto it, when the, some of the Masonic carpenters worked on building grandfather's house in 1878.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] The Crees house.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Crees house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, he was living with his third wife.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, but all of his children, you see, from each wife, and . . . well, that was it, they learned first hand what was going on and they could not tolerate it as good citizens. Allow it to happen, to mistreat the children. There were laws against it. And so they told the authorities. I don't know just which branch of the law it would be. If you were to go to report that, I really don't know what you'd call.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Were they living in the house while it was being built?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Or in another house, next door?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The house next door, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] And that was torn down afterwards.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that's the same house that's there now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] The one that they were building, yes. What kinds of things was she doing that they would take it to the law?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, for instance she tied my aunt Irene up to the bed post, naked, and beat her.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Things like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Child abuse.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, decidedly! And she was so mean to my uncle that he left home at 16. And I can't understand grandpa being quite so meek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Maybe she tied him up to the bed post and beat him while he was naked.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] That's a little speculation there. [laughter]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Grandpa was a wonderful man! Maybe he didn't have enough spunk, I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh my yes. He didn't die until 1911.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. How about his third wife, can you remember her?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes. She outlived him Oh yes. But all the girls hated her.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the grandkids. Did that hate get passed on to the.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they either weren't born or too little.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see. But now, that orchard, that walnut orchard [on Highland Ave. south of Lester Ave.] there? That was the Gragg walnut orchard.
bracketed_corrections: [on Highland Ave. south of Lester Ave.]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, don't get the Gragg and the Crees mixed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, and that's what I was trying to do. Was make sure I didn't mix them.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When you are ready for the walnut orchard I can tell you that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and I think we'll cover that in this. So now maybe is a good time to start going through the transcript from the previous recording. We were just. . . we talked first about George Witham?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oliver.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oliver Wit/jam, okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, his family was pioneers. And it might be that it often happens a successful man can't raise sensible kids. Businesslike kids. They just don't amount to a thing. They give them too much luxury. Let them escape real work, let them. . . so they know what they're doing. Because that's the way he acted. I know, some of the other Withams and the old man, his father, were respected by their neighbors. Oliver wasn't much. And let's see now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why didn't the neighbors respect him? Oliver, what kinds of things would.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, for one thing, he was kind of a clown. And he'd a make a fool of you if he could. And he didn't work hard, like most of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, at that time, people didn't respect you f you didn't work hard, or f you tried to. . . they made fun of you.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, or if you needed to work hard and didn't. He just didn't have an attitude that was likeable. Let's see now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now you mentioned that his wife was part Indian.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, but it was never mentioned.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: People didn't talk about it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. But anybody could see that she was. But she was a nice woman.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there any shame involved in that, that his wife was part Indian?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, in a way, yes. At that time there was. It was something that you usually wasn't proud of. And it shouldn't have been! Indians were there first, it was their land! And, give them some education and training, they can turn out to be very good citizens.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So without education and training, which they didn 't have before the whites came here, then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's right, didn't have the white-type education and training

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, by citizens you mean citizens by white standards, then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Yeah that's it. Now they thought it was pretty smart to be able to live off the land. Phil and I just think it's fun sometimes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, sometimes it's smart to have fin, maybe.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes! We think so don't we. [Laughter]. No, I had no complaint with Mrs. Witham. But in those days they had funny notions about what was commendable and what was looked down on, so, and being part Indian wasn't part of being good, great. But that's neither here nor there. There's a lot in your private opinion.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you know any other Indians in the neighborhood, other than Mrs. Witham?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes. I can't think of anyone in particular. But there were others too that were part Indian. It was quite common in those days.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: U/i huh. How about blacks, do you recall any black people at all?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't. . . hardly even saw one. Just practically nothing. Some in the city.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: By that you mean Corvallis?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm not sure, but I think I've seen one or two here. But it would be mostly bigger ones like Portland.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember when you saw your first black people? Was it like a curiosity, or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, as I remember it was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember where?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I think it was around Corvallis. I think it's probably in Corvallis. But I . . . they was very very scarce and I just really don't remember much about it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about Oriental people?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Chinese?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's all I know of was Chinese. Of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there very many in Corvallis in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not very many, but some. And they mostly worked in I believe in restaurants. What's that story somebody told me? Somebody. . I don't remember the circumstances, I think a . story was told. That there was black man in the crew of workers. It may have been farmers, I don't know. Anyway, they came in to lunch and had to wash up at the old pitcher pump. And the little boy of the family had never seen a black man. All eyes! And that guy noticed it. And when he got through scrubbing, he turned to the little boy, "Am I any whitah?" Scared him!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this was around Corvallis when you were a little girl?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, and somebody told that. You see, I never saw it happen, or didn't know who it happened to, but I heard that told. And it surprised the little boy so he jumped. And, let's see, about other. . . Oh, any other form of colored skin, negro and Chinese, I can't think of any others.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just a few Indians.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, but they were .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Mostly .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were, what do you call it, they belonged here. They weren't foreign. And let's see. Now what was this dumb thing? Oh, we had lots of foreign people. I mean from other countries. That came here and settled. For instance, in Clatsop County where I was born there was just oodles and oodles of Finns and Swedes and Norwegians. Lots and lots of

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: One thing I've noticed in doing these oral histories, is the Tortoras were from Italy, the Rohners were from Switzerland, there seems to have been a lot of Gennan, Swiss, Italian people that came around the turn of the century.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, yes, they were coming in pretty good.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know the reason for that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: To better their financial condition. Their economic condition.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well we were having a major depression here in the 1890's, but a lot of these people seem to have come about that time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Hmm. I don't know about that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember the Tortoras?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What can you remember about them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That they were Italian And I can't remember whether I saw any children my age, I remember middle life -- Tortoras in middle life. And they seemed to be nice, decent people.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the Rohners? Do you recall them.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I knew of them, of course. They were in business. What was that business? That wasn't the veterinarian, was it? Gosh, I'm not sure. But they were in some kind of business. People patronized them. We assimilated them anyhow.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were the foreign people that spoke with different accents or different languages were they treated any different?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, except some people laughed at the funny way they pronounced things. They had to have their jokes about them, but they accepted them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's see, let's. . . why don't we go back to.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What do you want to do here?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yep, we're on to. . . see you've got up here, you've got Mitzie Point.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] I put that on there. Okay. And Dimple Hill. That was a question I had. I talked with Edna Weise, and she says that Dimple Hill, what they call Dimple Hill now, used to be called Jackson Hill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, Locke's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was called Locke's Hill?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] No, no. Careful. Locke's Hill was where Chip Ross park is now, right? IV Hill? She said Locke's Hill became, was Dimple Hill, and that became IV Hill. Yeah, cause see you, you 'ye gotta be careful on using Dimple Hill. Because that's. . . she remembers Locke's Hill, which is IV Hill, which is Chip Ross Park.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I can't keep up with all the modem names and changes!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, right around 1940 I went through the maps and I found all these changes happened. And Edna Weise, I had the long talk with her, and she said the same.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now, she'd be more likely to get it right because I am getting forgetful. And she has a much younger brain than I have.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you can remember Dimple Hill being called Locke's Hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, because he's the one that owned it!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and Chip Ross Park, is that Locke's Hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Chip Ross Park goes clear around me, and I never did get caught up with it's history.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] We went out there, you and Francis and I went up there one day to have lunch or something, and there were signs all over the place. . . in fact a couple of years ago when it was so dry? And there were signs that we couldn't go in there because it was posted by the forest

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: department. Do you recall that? Because all we could do was go to the parking lot there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Hmm

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] It was up behind, it was up the hill behind where your father's farm was though. That was Locke's Hill. Did you ever hear the name Jackson Hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, sure. That's a different one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know where that was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let's see. And that was up Jackson Creek, the one that runs south of the High School, where is it, over here some where. And the Jackson's had left the community as citizens, as neighbors. Before we came.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you don 't remember the Jacksons?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, there was a couple, I think they were old bachelors. And they came out, they walked Out from town. They'd moved to town, and they'd walk out of town almost every day to the farm. And it was just not far from that 01 Witham place. Up the street a little. But I never met the . . . oh, yeah, I knew Mildred Jackson, she was in my grade. But I never met her parents.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know which hill is called Jackson Hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I think I do. But I have to be where I could point it out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Was it somewhere around Jackson Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, off to the southwest, I think Not very far.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Did you ever go up there on your horse?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And we had one neighbor on up the creek. But they, but the creek stayed in the ravine and the neighbor was on the side of the hill; that was Mr. Stoneback.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Which side of the hill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: North.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Yeah, there's a lot of open land up in that Jackson valley.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. It isn't good farm land at all. Mr. Stoneback didn't get to first base farming.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What nationality was he?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, he was just a mixture American.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh. Stoneback, though.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall a family named Robinson in that area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that was earlier generation. Yes. I never met the person. Now, my mother knew a lot of these old timers in the generation before me. Robinson and them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] What did Stoneback farm up there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, he didn't have a very big farm and he didn't have much open ground, it was mostly trees. And it was not rich at all. And he just existed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was he on the Robinson's old place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I really don't know. That one has to be looked up in the County courthouse.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] When you went up to Jackson Hill, how did you go from the farm?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I don't remember if I could go on my pony or not. And if I didn't, I walked.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Do you remember anything about it back when you were a kid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't. It didn't seem to leave an impression.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. That was about half my questions, right there. I was going to ask about the Knott's too, but I think we're in here, so as we go through the pages here we can probably get the Knotts and the Owens a little bit.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now, we gotta be awful careful about the Knotts. Remember, this man has descendants still living.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, that goes back to the first settlers, the Knotts. They were at the same time as the Robinsons. Do you recall any of the older Knotts then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know whether that was the Knotts we knew, that was there when we came, or whether it was his father. I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What can you remember about that family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, he was an awful nice man. But he didn't have family help or any other kind of help. And he didn't get much of anywhere with his farming. And his wife made a little silly sissy of his boy instead of teaching him to be a rugged little helper. For heaven's sake, everybody was talking about it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you say making him a sissy, was it kind of like some of these pictures we've been looking at.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah!! Lotta hair and girl clothes and all that rot. And just making him his attitudes and everything sissy instead of making him rugged. And a helper for his father on the farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We looked at a picture of one of your uncles or cousins that was dressed up in girl's clothes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, that was my aunt's neighbor.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, it was a neighbor.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And I used to play with him when I'd go to visit her.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, did that hurt him when he got older? When he got older, did that hurt him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what became of him. But I don't think so. I never heard of it. I don't know whether they moved away or not. But anyway his father had a bakery at that time, in Corvallis.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, we were talking about Dear Abby, how she had a column in the paper about a woman who was ruining her boy by.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you said it was pretty common when you were a little girl.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes! My land, it was the style! Crazy style. [Laughter]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many families do you think raised their little boys as girls at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, those that I knew wasn't more than two or three, but I heard of others and I've heard of lots of. . . I heard it commented about, it was just done.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would people that didn't raise their little boys as girls think that that was a bad thing?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, very much.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Where did they get the idea?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they do it before the 1890's?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know how far back it went.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember when they stopped doing it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it don't sound like they've stopped yet. [Laughter] Well, my little brother didn't get raised that way. He got to be taught to work. And I did too. I didn't mind working. But I wanted some other thing along with it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So when the Knotts or the families that did raise their boys as girls, you think that they did that, they didn 't teach the kids to work enough, was one of the problems.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes, it was one of the problems. Most definitely. And a farmer, most farmers, and any other poor people, can't afford to make sissies of their children and give them money like a rich person, luxuries. It just can't be done. They haven't got it. So they better teach him how to live without it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it wasn't just that they. [END OF TAPE]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I don't know if we got that in there, but I hope we did.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now there's the Kings. Nobody could be poorer. But nobody could have been more wonderful than the family.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now that's the Sol King family.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: His grandchildren.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They were fairly poor then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes. Hard to have 10 kids. Cost something to feed 10 kids. But they were just wonderful kids. They were the ones that got me started on botany.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Well, how did they get started?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They had to make their own fun. And those kids would go out and make a game of it. And it just worked great, just worked great.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So a lot of the interest you got in nature was from the Kings and a lot of the interest they got in nature was strictly because they didn 't have money.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's right. They had to make their own fun and they had the brains to do it. And, now, I could have lived there 100 years and my folks would never have taught me anything about botany. They didn't know much in the first place in botany. But you see when they were so busy and had such problems of their own, business problems, that isn't the right word, what is it, economic problems. So busy with that they don't think much of wasting time on aesthetic things. They think it's wasting time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How important do you think aesthetics are?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They are very important in the right amounts. Can't go all that way, of course. But there ought to be an introduction to it, some introduction. Some kids have natural ability. And when they get a little introduction to something they can get onto it and go on from there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about college, is that too late?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. It'd be fme if they had the money to get to it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think people taking, like I took forestiy, do you think I should be taking classes in aesthetics, do you think that would be a good thing for kids?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no. You can mix it in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just with other classes, not.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But, people like my dad just thought it was nonsense. But see there was 19 kids in his family. Of course some of them died in infancy. And they didn't have much money for aesthetics. So you've got to teach them that it is important but they have to get mostly for themselves. And so the King kids did. And they turned out something wonderful. Every last one of them. Of course the oldest boy, he had to go to the first world war. And he didn't come back till late in life. He'd had enough work on the farm.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ah ha! He got a chance to get out.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And the oldest girl she got to be a teacher when she was in her late teens, and she felt so sorry for her mother and the rest of the family, she spent her whole life helping them. Just stayed single and was a teacher. She was just wonderful. She lived to be 98.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The rest of them married, I don't think there was any more bachelors or maids. One of them just my age, we were great pals. And they did not have time to run around and play much. They made education or some use of it out of the play. Like the botany. They learned from things and they didn't have any books, they couldn't get the scientific names so they made them up. You bet your life.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, I think we talked about it before, but I want to make sure we got that in there. We were talking about ethno-botany, and you were talking about making up names, and we were talking about a plant called 'twooly britches, Hydrophyllum capitatum."

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
