entries.text: Was that a made up name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I guess so. It started as far as I know with my paternal grandmother. She learned that it was good to eat, so she used it instead of chard. She didn't have any, I suppose she had some chard in her garden sometimes, but this was free and there to pick. And good to eat, so she used it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How important were wild plants to the pioneers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, pretty important. Because at first they didn't have the place to make a good garden, and they could use these wild things. But they didn't know how lucky they were, that they had it. And then later on, when things were more easy, everybody had as much as everybody else, they looked down on the wild ones. That makes me mad.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was kind of like looking down on farmers maybe, looking down on the poorer ltfe style?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: All those things have their proper place and they ought to be appreciated.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So when they got enough money then they stopped eating.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wild plants.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And here we eat it just for fun. Just to show we can pick the right ones!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] I have some yampah [Perideridia ore gana/ at home I was gonna bring you and forgot it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh? Where did you find it?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Oh, it grows all over the hills out here, and there's a lot of it this year.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Really.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Yeah. A lot of it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What do you know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you like yampah?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, you bet. I had the most wonderful steak dinner once, over in eastern Oregon with some friends, relatives of my son-in-law. He got the steak and he cooked it. He cooked the whole works in fact. And I dug the yampah. And they liked it! It is one of the best one, wild plants, don't you think so? More to it!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about camas [Camassia leichtlinii]?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah. That's fine too. But we don't have much of that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What do you think we. . . do you think we should grow it for people to eat, so they know what it tastes like?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, not necessarily. But if we insist on eating it, we ought to also raise it, because it would soon deplete the whole country of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you think of any good camas patches?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not in this valley.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are they mostly gone?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. In eastern Oregon there's patches of them. Lots.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the orchards? We were talking about those, and we mentioned the Gragg walnut orchard. You wanted to talk some more about that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Do you want to get that now?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, let's maybe go through this.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Yeah, you keep distracting her. Okay, yeah, let's go on with the transcript here, and we'll come back up on it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Go through those and see if there was anything there you want to. Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well. This hasn't many corrections.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Page 2.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [Reading from transcript] "There were several different ones that ended up with the Holbrooks. And my brother George bought it from them. By that time we children were grown, and we bought that from, and he bought that from Mrs. Holbrook. Her husband had died, and she had six kids." "How big were these farms?" "Papa's was 200 and the Holbrooks was 50. The Withams was probably 200 or more, and Stoneback was probably 100." . . . "Do you recall any families in the Soap Creek Area?" "No, I don't, except Sam Moore who soon moved to Corvallis." At the turn of the century, yeah. And I didn't know the Marcks or the Olsons, but I'd heard of them. And Neva was in my grade.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That would be Neva Olson?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Neva Moore.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Neva Moore? Okay. Was that Neva Lauridson?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, she never married.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Wildes. Yes I knew Francis Wildes. And I think she was in my grade. I knew she came from out north here somewhere. I heard of Carters, wouldn't know the Carters, but that name is familiar.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember a Grandma Carter?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. All I remember is Grandma Frazier.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, that Frazier Creek is named after?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now can you tell me about Grandma Frazier?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You bet. Shall we do it now or later?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Sure, might as well do it. I don't think we 'ye got her in the transcript, I don 't think we mentioned her before.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well now, before we came here, the Fraziers, when Mr. Frazier was living, lived in this area, farmed in this area. I don't know where his farm was but I presume it was up there off Tomlin loop on Frazier Creek. I presume that's where it was. Anyway, I didn't know him. But after we came here, Mr. Frazier was dead. And Grandma was living with her single son, Jim, and Sam was married and living with his family, and they both lived back in, along Frazier Creek, on what is called Tomlin Loop now. And I would go riding around sometimes on my pony and stop in. And she got to telling me pioneer stories. And she sure told me a dilly. And I'd heard of it in history. She had come out in '57 in a wagon train, ox teams. And her girlfriend and her family were along. When they came to Utah, the girlfriend and some more people divided the train, and went south to California. And the Fraziers came on to Oregon. And they got in to the Mountain Meadow Massacre in Utah. And you know that thing tried to be; an awful lot of people tried to keep it hush hush. Not let it get out, and all the facts known. But it was, that kind of fixed it. Because the people who fought the whites were dressed as Indians and fixed up as Indians, and they weren't, they were Mormons!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Mountain Meadow Massacre was Mormons dressed as Indians?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You bet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] And it was the girlfriend's part that got into it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And she was, her whole family was killed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Her girlfriend's family was killed during that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, this is Mrs. Frazier? Grandma Frazier's girlfriend.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And can you remember any details that she described from that massacre?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, like the one's that killed them were dressed as Indians, and they weren't. And evidently somebody lived to tell some of them, because she said that the baby was shot from her mother's arms, things like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Grandma Frazier wasn't there. They came north.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They came north.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So she must have come by way of the Applegate Trail.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I'm mixed up on those trails. I don't know the route.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Did she give any, did Grandma Frazier tell anything about the trip from Utah here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not particularly. Evidently it was nothing spectacular. But I don't know about the trails. I wish I did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did she talk about Klamath Falls at all, or southern Oregon, or Eugene?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you're not sure what route she took?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Remember any other tales she told?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Have I told you any? [To Phil]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] I remember that one, but I don't remember others.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was the main one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the reason that the Mormons dressed as Indians? What was the reason they were attacking the wagon train?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: To blame it on the Indians!!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why did they want to do that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Why shouldn't they? They didn't want the world to think they did it!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so they were just simple thieves, and they were just covering their tracks.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah! [very emphatic]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They weren't trying to get anything politically going against Indians or anything.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no, no. You couldn't get much political going with Indians in those days! They didn't take to politics!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall any of her other stories, about maybe when she first got here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I wish I did. But that was before and right at 18 -- 1905. Yes, if I'd have been a little more historically minded, I would have had her tell me about when they lived there, you know. How life was and all that. But I didn't. I missed a lot things.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you know any other pioneers that have crossed on the Oregon Trail? Have you talked to any others?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Who have I talked to? Not right now I don't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. So Grandma Frazier is the only actual.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: One that I'm sure of. And her two sons were two of the men that helped put in Highland Way. That had to be done free by the citizens. But in a year or two, they moved on. I don't know where they went or anything. Never heard of them again.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Fraziers.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so, there are no Fraziers around anymore?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh uh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they helped build Highland Way and then shortly after that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Then they beat it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it was about 1907 or 1908.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, more like 1906. Yeah, I'd like to have kept track of all of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did Grandma Frazier leave with them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see. So you are one of the last people around to know the Fraziers. At least while they were here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Urn hmm

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, I've got you digressing again here. On page 2.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well anyway, that's about all of page 2.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Hummm. [Reading transcript] "The Witham girl was older than I. Then on the south toward town was the King family from the King's Valley family of Solomon King." I wonder if I ought . . where's my pen. Thank you. Hadn't I better say this through their . son Abe?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Through Abe King? Well, one thing we can check on the genealogy, or like you say, we can check on land ownership patterns.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I know that Abe was their father, and Abe was Solomon's son.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see, so that Abe King. . . well that's one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Abe King 's farm down there near where you lived. That's the advantage of having this tape recorder going, too. You don't have to write it, you can just say you want to make that point.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So Sol King was on Abe King 's. . . his father was Abe King from the King's Valley Kings, and then he named one of his sons Abe King also.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Well, the one from King's Valley was Solomon, and Abe was his son.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] And then it was Abe 's children you played with.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it was Abe's children, Solomon's grandchildren.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know anything about the politics then? I'm assuming if his name was Abe, he was named after Abraham Lincoln.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't know who he was named after. I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you know anything about the Mount Union people being. . . any civil war stories from around?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't remember any civil war stories.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Page 4.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [Long pause as she reads] Now why didn't I put what it is? "Just a little one room building. Don't know when it was first built." The school.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Here's page 5.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This seems to be all pretty good.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You've been pretty thorough in your comments here, too.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: "You had to go where the owners said you had to go." "If somebody made a diagonal across their field, they made you follow a fence line." That was naughty.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What's that? The diagonal across the field?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Did you ever happen to get chided for that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. Because I couldn't go with my horse, I had to walk, and I didn't do any harm. And there were no crops in that pasture where I went.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now that's. . . we were talking about the field, the road that come off by the [Good Samaritan] hospital. Is that the right-of-way?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Now, when you went to school in Corvallis, you went right over the ridge into town, didn't you? Or did you go out to Highway 99 and down?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I went 99.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] You did?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. It sort of parallels the road that goes in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you took that route out.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, just walking. But sometimes, quite a lot of times, we diagonaled out into the pasture instead of keeping along Mr. Knott's fence. Because here came the King kids down this way. We met them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see, so you'd meet with the King kids.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] So they would come down then the north side of the hill to join that same route to go down to the highway?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Okay. Well, why didn't you just go across where their place was and on down into town and to the south?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we didn't go to town. We went to that little school.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Oh that's right, that little school. Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And when we did go to town, at that time, you see the road was put through that papa and Tressure and all of them made.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Oh that one. Do you recall anybody named "Drum" or "Stout" that was in that area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I've heard of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. I think they 're back with the Robinsons.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Probably.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, they're earlier. Let's see, we're on page 6 here. So, "Yes. Four years." You've added, before you went to college, okay. I think people will be fairly clear.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, well I hope so. I thought I had them fixed so they made sense.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now where you 'ye crossed out things, like here we're on page 7, and you've put in other words, is that a correction or you just don't want these printed?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's a correction.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Here, for instance: "Mr. William Knotts," and it has two t's, "was the owner and resident there. And Tom Owens was one of his grandchildren. And owns the place now." Because his mother inherited it or got it somehow. And he inherited it from her.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, when we come across these crossed out areas, would it be all right just to put your comments in parentheses, so somebody reading it knows that that's been pencilled in later?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, unless you just.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh would you prefer having it just look like a book? We'll do it however you want.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Well, you do whatever you think's best there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we'll just use. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: "And we. . . he let us have a route through his place for a while on a certain place and he

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: changed it." See we went through his woods back of the Holbrook place. Then he changed that and it was clear over out by Berry Hill toward the Hospital.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the landowner could tell people. . . he couldn 't keep you off the land but he could tell you which route to take through it?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Do you know why he did it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, he couldn't keep us from going through if we couldn't get through otherwise.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Why did he change it? Do you know?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. For one thing, the surrey wheels were cutting quite good ruts. And it come out right close to his house and used his driveway up and down the hill And it might be we was cutting it up too much. I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did it create any animosity or ill feelings when he changed it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. It just was his right to tell you which way to go on it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: "Where the opposite the property." I don't know whether that "the" needs to come out or not. "Where opposite the property where the hospital is on the south side of it."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'll circle that one right there. That could just be a typo on the part of the person doing the transcription.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, might be something else should have been written, I don't know. "As you go out ninth street a little way, I mean the highway here" down here, "as you go out there and come to that ridge." Now, what's that?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Where the hospital is. Yeah, I think we're talking about going out to Ninth street to the ridge on the hospital there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: "Yes, the other side of the hospital, along the line of the fence, of the Knotts place." Some of them goes east on the top of the hill on my father's place, Owens now. "You can still see the tracks going east along the fence and turning to the right or south."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, those tracks are still there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that would be Knotts 'first route that he put through the property?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The second route.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The second route. Okay, that would be.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I want a piece of paper. I want to make a drawing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Now we 're drawing on the back of page 7 here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now, on this I'm gonna put a dot. And that's at the top of the hill above the old farm where my dad's place comes. And then here's Locke's Lane. He sold off of his place to Locke.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so from the top of the hill at your dad's place, Locke's Lane is going due east.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now, Locke's Lane follows Mr. Knott's line fence.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Then that would be going west.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Highland Way, there's Highland Way coming along there. And here's . . . I'm making awful faint lines. And on this side of the fence is where I went down. See, I walked along the fence. But when Mr. Knotts didn't want us to go in his woodsy place anymore, and we had this road, oh no, before we got this road, he let us go down along his fence where I walked. But there had to be a gate here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Where was the school?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Down here on the highway, edge of the road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] So it was off in the direction toward where the hospital was.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was on the south side of the road going to the hospital.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Before you came to the ridge or over the ridge?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the ridge was . . where am I? .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, here's the top of your dad's hill, and here's

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah, here we are. The ridge I'm talking about comes out to the road and abruptly stops. But we were here to where we're going. Now these were the lines where I used to walk, it's the track that we went. And when we come to this ridge we had to turn like this, on the west side of the road, you see. And it's right around this turn where you can see those tracks yet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, where would the hospital be now, compared to those tracks?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Back up here somewhere.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so this is right before you get to the road, where this turn is?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, the road goes by here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Highway 99.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And that's where you see the tracks. And then this ridge abruptly stops here somewhere, I guess it's just down to the level, I forget how it is. But that's where we had to go, around that turn.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When did he make you start going this way?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not very long. . . sometime between 1902 and 1905.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So these tracks then would be from 1902 to 1905 when these were put in there?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Starting then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, about that time. And they've been there ever since.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Is this because of the. . . you were saying the surrey cut into the ground.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, but somehow this track. . . I guess when they made the highway wider they cut off the end of it or something. It stops abruptly, you look at it next time you go by.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know where those tracks are, Phil?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] No, they should be just right south of the ftnce line there, though, right?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Mr. Knotts's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Yeah, you went along Mr. Knotts '5 fence line, but.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When we. . . yes, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] On the north side or south side?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It would be the south side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Oh, okay. Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But, I think when you can see it, you can see how that little ridge, it's a ridge here, it's a little hill, it soon disappears into thin air.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that ftnce line still there?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Well that's along the north side of the farm, right?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, this is Mr. Knotts's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] I mean the south side of the.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, this is Mr. Knotts's. This is Highland Way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And we could not go to our school with horses or, well. . . because there were gates, and they're usually big heavy miserable things and I couldn't open them. But when I went to town, you see, I could go on the highway. No gates. Then we had no need to go this way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did people just stop using that, then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Highland went in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] So you only used that for a few years down there, then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not more than two I don't think. Something like two.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This might be the last. . . we found ruts going back probably to the Applegate Trail days, but these might be the only ruts that were for surreys and only from surreys that are still left in the County. I can 't think of any others.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there may be of course. I couldn't make that statement. But I still look every time I go by!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] . . . since the last surrey went through those ruts, right, and you can see what happens. But there's still a sign there, then it shows the wagon track will hang around a centuty. I mean it wasn't wagon track even, it was just a surrey.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was a real steep little pull. Just a real steep little pull.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] So you had to come down in there and then turn and go up over the steep pull.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was no. . . after we got around that turn we were down on the highway level.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think that wagon, that iwo years of surrey travel through that one little area had a permanent impact on the vegetation?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just where the track is. But you see the weeds are coming up the track. I used to be able to see it a lot plainer. I'm trying to remember . . . if my father went over that ridge with his wagon. See we didn't use it many years, then Highland Way was opened. And that was a devil for the horses, just an awful pull.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Highland Way was.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, the tracks. Highland Way had some pretty good pulls, but not as bad as that. Now I can't remember, when it was, or which way we went, but I think it was after Highland Way was put in. But it may have been before it. That Papa used to sell wood in town to the people for their stoves and things. And I tell you that's a slow job. You can't go out of the walk. And it takes you all day to take a load of wood to town and come back. And so he used fill up two wagons, and put the old team on the second wagon, and I drove it. Because you see those horses were trustworthy. And he took the young frisky ones. And I don't know whether we went around those tracks or Highland Way, which it was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, the route that was older, the one that Knott had you stop using, are there any traces of that track?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I imagine there are, but I haven't been in there since.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know which way that goes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, sure.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you describe it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [Laughter] Well, you see the Holbrook place. It belongs to my nephew now; we had to go through it. And then we came to Mr. Knotts's oak woods, which his house was surrounded with in the back. And go through that. Out to the driveway that he used for his home.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's still there now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. As you get acquainted with .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] That route is still there. When we went out there a couple of years ago, and Frances [Stilwell] and I walked back there. That old road comes through. It goes from the gate, it would be Holbrook now, it makes a bit of a gentle S turn before it comes up where the house was.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh huh. You saw it then?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Yes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I haven't been back to see it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that's the old.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that was the old route.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think that's the one the pioneers used when they hit Jackson-Frazier wetlands and went up and connected to the Highland Road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] That's going back to 1850's. Well Highland Road wasn't there then. Hilltop Road was about in there in 1853.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] But it wasn't a road, per Se. Not in our sense, no.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What have I got to say about that?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: If you 'ye got anything to say, now is the time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I don't quite understand what the question is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, what I was trying to explain is the 1853 maps show Hilltop Road where Highland Way is now. And then it showed a route going out around what we call the Jackson Frazier wetlands, back in 1853. So people traveling out of Corvallis that hit those wetlands, went up the route we've been talking about, and connected to a road that was called Hilltop Road. In 1853. And that's what became Highland Way in 1905.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] So what did they do, they went up sort of like up where Highway 99 is now till they got to sort of the ridge the hospital is on and then turned west to go around that marshy area down there? Yep.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] And so then they would go out off toward where her father's farm was? And through Robinsons. And then, the routes we're talking about are really old routes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Back up towards Lewisburg then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What was that about Lewisburg?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] He's saying that when the wetlands down there got too wet, they would turn off up the ridge there where the hospital is now and head out toward your father's farm, just loop around the whole thing to the west. And then come back to Lewisburg and go on. The old route in there, where all those old marshes were, were described as lakes and slews and marshes, that was back when the Stouts and the Robinsons and the Cooks lived there, and so that route that you were taking before Knotts changed your route, that was the first wagon road through that area, back to the 18. . . You were saying you wish you knew where those old routes were, you were on them according to the old maps.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] But that would only have been used when it was wet, and everything was flooded, right? Yeah, as a connector road. But the upper road would have been used all the time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I would have thought they would use Lewisburg Road. That's the one that goes to Sulphur Springs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, they would have used that, and they would have gone through Mulkeys and Withams property, and part of Walnut, but then people coming north of town from Corvallis along what became 9th Street, zf it got too wet they'd have to cut over to that road. So that's how they would cut back up on that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They couldn't come out 9th Street and hit Lewisburg Road at Mountain View then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Only when it was too wet. Otherwise they could. That's an old route through there. But when it's too wet they 'd have to cut up the same route that you were taking to come to school. They would have to take that up to go to.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They'd have a job; they'd have some gates to open.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. [Pause]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, let's see.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Page 8.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What do you want to talk about?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Anything you see in there that you want to change or add or subtract, or. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: "Did you have a name to it, that right of way, or just called it the. . ." Answer is "you just called it by the name of the owner of the property, Knotts, or Griggs, or whatever." "And those tracks are still there." That's what we were talking about. "And they predate 1905. Yes."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And I think you've added a lot of good detail to it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: "It probably was 1905 but the road didn't get through so it could. . . it was usable that first year." Oh, that's Highland Way. . . that they made it, only in spots. Little sections. Yes, probably 1906 until that old right of way was dumped." "Was that the remains of that right of way, that you know?" "Yes."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and page 9?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: "That's all you can see, yes." "Did you pay much attention to how when they stopped using a road how maybe the vegetation filled in, what types of plants began growing in the old road or. ." "Yes, I was more or less observant of it because I was interested in botany." "Can you kind of describe what you noticed with that?" "Well, weeds and grass came pretty soon. And the nice flowers like spring beauties that he has a picture of, they didn't. . they . were a little more delicate and harder to do anything . . . I mean they are more liable to be not able to compete with the bad stuff, weeds and things." "Are you calling weeds, exotic plants brought into the area?" "No, really. Weeds, some of the wild mustards, and things in the daisy family and buttercups and dandelions and those thistle things. They are very prolific and they take over." "When you went to Sulphur Springs, was that just a destination, a place to turn around and come back or did you do things when you got there?" "For a while in earlier days, families camped there and picnicked on weekends. You see, that was a public picnic ground because of the springs. Public used it quite a bit in those days. Went there and camped. In later years it fell prey to modern vandals."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Phil, you had a question there on Sulphur Springs. The, calling a plant "ladyslipper"?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Mountain ladyslippers. Like out at the Smith place.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: One of the rarest things we had.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Cvpripedium montanum. But that's a different. . . because I've talked to quite a few people since I talked to you last, and they said, well, the ladyslippers grow in with the old growth and the ladyslippers are real important and they talked about ladyslippers that are still off the side of the road on the way to Mary's Peak, but that's a different flower isn't it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think those are the little pink one's aren't they?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But so, okay, is there some clarification on this?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Yeah, you remember the big white ones from up at Sulphur Springs, though, don't you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have transplanted a few to my mother's yard, and they all died, and I'm sorry.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Sony for transplanting them or sorry that they died?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, because I didn't know that they wouldn't live then. "Are there any soda springs around here?" "No, not that I've heard of this side of Sodaville."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, here's page 10.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: "Not right around here. There's one at Cascadia. It's just where they were, but people did camp there. When we came here in 1900, that summer I remember my grandfather and his family was out there camping at Sulphur Springs, and we went over there and visited one

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Sunday with horses and surrey of course." "How long would people camp, for a day or two or a week?" "Oh, they'd camp for a week sometimes." "Would they do anything besides drink the water?" "I don't know what they did. I explored of course, explored for wildflowers. There were special ones in that area. And I did drink the water because I thought if I came that far I should drink some of it. It was supposed to be good for one's health. Didn't care for the taste too well." "It must have helped you, you're pretty healthy several years later. That's what they always claimed would happen." "Maybe that's the secret of it, I don't know." "Maybe we'll get more people going there to drink the water now." "Grandpa had a tent and was camping there and of course, when we went there was no such a thing as a car at that time so we had to go with a surrey with a fringe on top and two horses and that was quite a trip over that Sulphur Springs Hill, it's pretty rugged, pretty rough." "Had that road been in for quite a while?" "Yes." "Could people take bicycles over the road or would they hike in without buggies?"

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] When you were going up there, did you start early in the morning, or how long did it take you to go over to Sulphur Springs.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, I didn't go till after breakfast.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Yeah, but that's a farmer's breakfast. How early is breakfast?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Kinda early! And that'd take all day.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, Charlie Olson said that when that road came out over Lewisburg Saddle there; he's 95 and Wanda Cook is 95, and they both lived out in that area and I've talked with both of them. And there 's some contention about when that road went in there. But he said that the road angled out, it came through Sol King's place, and went out past the walnut orchard. Would that be the Gragg walnut orchard that he was talking about? The old road that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Gragg walnut orchard didn't go in until 1914.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: 1914. Was there another walnut orchard out in that area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no papa's was the first.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Now there's a walnut orchard on Soap Creek Road, on the Govier's place. Do you know anything.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Goviers, yeah I know the Goviers. Not well, but I know of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Uh huh. Do you know anything about why people were putting walnut orchards in or what earlier orchards there could have been?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, because there weren't enough to supply the market here then. It would have been a good cash crop you see.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it was a cash crop. But the home orchards that people had, apples and pears.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was no. . . this was english walnuts. All the walnuts in those orchards were the old fashioned black walnut, and the butter nut. But they never had a big orchard, just one or two trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that was the difference between a commercial orchard and a family orchard.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh huh. In those days a family orchard was just one or two trees and black walnut.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about, we found a chestnut tree in one of the old orchards.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, somebody would bring in a chestnut tree. We never had one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Back to the idea that you were coming in from Soap Creek, after you went over the pass and came down then, it would come out by your father's orchard.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not until 1905. It went on down to Mountain View and the highway.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] At Lewisburg Road, yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: At Lewisburg Road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] But then after. . . now one of the things that you mentioned once before that I'm not clear

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: on, after Highland went in, how would the route from the pass, coming down the hill, was Highland pretty much where it is now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] 0/cay. So they would come right down off of the hills and angle over to where Highland is. Or would they take the Lewisburg Road out and turn down Highland.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it was no connection between Lewisburg Road, north of the high school, and Highland At that time, there wasn't a road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] So Highland, really then, went off up toward the pass?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, angled northwest.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Yeah. Across where the high school is now. Or north of there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, no on papa's road, on the way it is now, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, there's a question I have on that then, too. Where did it cross the creek, Jackson Creek? And where did it cross Frazier Creek, and how did it cross?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Map.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're gonna draw a map on page 11.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let's see. Jackson Creek comes out of the little Jackson valley. Wiggles around, I won't wiggle it. And

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the upper left hand side of the page.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Mr. Stoneback's place was up here. And the creek was down here in the valley. And let's see. My distances won't be right. But anyway, north of the Witham place it turns south, almost right corner, and a bridge.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right there at Withams?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And Withams house is up here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so this is Stonebacks in the upper left hand corner? And Williams is south?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wait a minute, wait a minute, I should put that in first. He was back up here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so Withams off the page here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, Witham is on the page and Stoneback is off.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] But he was north of the creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. He was north of the creek yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay now, where the creek turns real sharp and this bridge is in there, was that an old bridge?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh uh! They hadn't put that in yet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did people. . could people cross there before they put the bridge in? Was there a natural

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: crossing or anything there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: As I remember the banks were pretty high. Be a devil of a job to cross.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Was that just to get into Withams place or on up. to Stonebacks as well?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, this turned here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so when people came up before the bridge was built, they would have to come up past Withams and towards Stonebacks, come way back up the valley there to get across the creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let's see now. Humm. I don't know. Huh. To go to Stonebacks you had to go straight up from the bridge, and then you turned this way to go to Toilmans And Fraziers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Toilnians and Fraziers were north of Stonebacks.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes. Huh. I didn't leave enough room on my paper.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But we could say the old route maybe went by Withams, came up the creek to Stonebacks.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it never followed the creek. Oh it did follow the creek in a way. But it was quite a little ways from the creek up here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it'd follow up along the base of the hill then, above the creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. And then it went to Toilmans?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, but the road went to Toilmans, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I wish I'd have started down here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, we can start over.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'd better. Yes. Going in front of my dad's place the road [Crescent Valley Drive] went straight west.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Then it made a turn around the little pasture where Mrs. Witham picked strawberries in. Then it turned to the left and went through the gate and ended at Withams. And up Jackson Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] So that's the road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. And it has to go farther west and turn to the north and go up a hill and to Withams.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And then, now this is the. . . Jackson Creek should be right along in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it crossed Jackson Creek right by her strawberry patch in here somewhere?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. There's the bridge.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now was that a real old crossing in there, or did they just build that crossing?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't remember about it. Because there's no highway, this wasn't used. . . they all went up Lewisburg Road to get anywhere up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Okay now, where. . . put your father's farm there, and then where did the new Highland Road go?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh [mumbling] then down here a ways and then north to Toilman's lane, and Frazier Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was the new route?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Uh huh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, but the old route went way on back to Withams and stuff first.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, that one was just private. Stoneback and Witham.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see, so Stoneback and Witham were the only ones that used that, other people didn't go that way. Okay.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Now when they built Highland, that's what I was wondering about, when they.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, down here the roads.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Okay, now where did the road come down from Sulphur Springs from the pass? How did that connect?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that just went straight through to Mountain View. As Lewisburg Road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Okay. Just the way it does now.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Then when they. . . how did they connect it with Highland?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they couldn't do it here, there was no road there for years and years. Well, a road came off of it to come down past Toilmans. [This sounds like the current Crescent Valley Drive.] Well, I guess ours went up to it, yes, Highland Way. It was very crooked, you see. Yeah, Lewisburg's close up here, and this crooked road runs into it. Then when this road was put through from Lewisburg, I mean Lewisburg Road, it hit Highland. Then they was pretty well fixed for roads.
bracketed_corrections: [This sounds like the current Crescent Valley Drive.]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] When did they do that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't remember what year. It was quite a bit after this one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] So when you went up to Sulphur Springs then, you went off up this road and then up past Tollman 's place? That s' what 1 was getting at.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I had to hit Lewisburg Road to get to Sulphur Springs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you went all the way out to the highway? Then up to Lewisburg?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no, I got in here somehow. Because there's a Mr. Morse lived here on the corner of Lewisburg and. . . and what would be. Oh, Highland Way. There was a private road, or some kind of road, you see. The neighbors could get in and out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Their name was Morris?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Morse, M-o-r-s-e.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And she was Mrs. Toliman's sister. And Toilman's were the ones that had the 17 or 18 year old girl that got killed with a Model T. She didn't treat it quite right, and it jumped around and fell over.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When she was only l7or 18?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there's the Toilmans, the Morses, the Stonebacks, the Witliams, and the Graggs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
