entries.text: Now, another thing that we're noticing is the animal life, a lot of it is scarcer. See when we first came in here there weren't so many people, whereas there's hunting. And I don't suppose there's very strict laws about not hunting. But we soon made certain things scarcer by not conserving, or being careful with them. And one of them was the native grouse. But I've got some of his feathers!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So most of the native grouse are. . . there's not so many now.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, my, no. And they've gone farther back in the woods. And when we came they were roosting in our orchard.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] So they were down in the valleys then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, bet your life.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did they call them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well that was the common name. I don't know any other name. Do you?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just grouse?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. But it wasn't the Russ grouse. It was a different kind, smaller. A little smaller.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever hear them called pheasant?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we left that for the China pheasants.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, just the China pheasant was the only thing you called pheasant.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Urn hmm. And they at one time were thick. And then some fool brought in foxes. And that was the end of the pheasants. Because the fox got their nests on the ground. They didn't know half what they thought they knew or they'd never have brought a fox around.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Do you remember blackberries?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Do I!! You bet!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] What kind of blackberries?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well they were just the little ones, I don't know any other names, just the small type of wild blackberry [Rubus uvsinus]. That was the good one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] The native one.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. That was one. And then people brought in himalayas [Rubus procerus], and what's that other big one?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Evergreen?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. Oh, no no. That was native

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Himalaya and the lance leaf, the real divided leaf one [Rubus laciniatus].

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, and they got.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] When did that happen?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I think at that time I was a young married . . . I wasn't a kid anymore. And it got loose from civilization. It

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Would have been in the teens, then, right?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So people brought that in around maybe World War I?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You know, I didn't know I was gonna have to talk about the times. [Laughter] I don't remember the dates. But it runs in my head that I was about . . . the kids were little, you know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] So how old were you then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was . . . between 30 and 40 I imagine.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] That's when the blackberries were brought in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, not the ones that are here now. I mean the good ones.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] The himalayas, you know.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Those kind, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] When you were between 30 and 40.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Well they've made a lot of headway in a short time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You bet. Oh, blackberries, well mercy. I have to go out all the time and cut those little ones, you know, the good ones. They come out and they just take over here. I betcha they make runners thirty feet long.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] The native ones you're talking about?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about poison oak [Rhus diversiloba]? Can you remember so much poison oak when you were a kid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah. It was in our oak woods.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there's always been a lot of poison oak then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes. And I don't get it enough to really matter. But boy, some of my neighbors .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] There was a fellow wrote a letter to the Gazette Times about the blackberries, and he was an old timer, he'd be in his ,nid-80 's now I guess, but he said when he was a kid growing up, he said, he was talking mainly about rivers, the Alsea river, and management along the river, and he

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: said when he was a kid they let the cattle graze right down to the water's edges and we didn't have blackberries all over the place. Talking about these himalayan blackberries. And I happened to think well that's because when he was a kid there weren't any himalayan blackberries around here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no, they got loose from cultivation, you see. And if you let them go, they're just terrible.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about bachelor buttons [Centaurea cyanus]? We didn't talk about that before.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, bachelor. . . well weren't they brought in as a garden flower?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Yeah, as a flower garden thing.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. A yard flower

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] You told a story about one of the neighbor's wives that put in bachelor buttons, or something. You can repeat that f you want to. Was that in here?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] I don 't know whether it's in there or not.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it was brought in as a yard flower. And I don't know what year, but I think before the turn of the century.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think maybe even back to the 1840's. It was one of the first ornamental flowers brought in I think.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Umm And it is a pretty flower, but. It's the kind that makes itself into a weed. And it's in the daisy family and that's still worse. And. . . now we lived in Clatsop County at first, that was very primitive and unsettled. And one of our neighbors, woman, had some of those flowers in her yard. And my dad saw, and he told her that out in the valley here that was a terrible pest in the crops. And he advised her to destroy it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Did she?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. I believe she was peeved at papa.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall how they began controlling it in the valley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they couldn't control it very well because it reseeded itself so nicely, and it was mostly in the grain. Now, in a garden you could control it. But not in a grain field! You couldn't go in there and pull every last one of them, you couldn't take machinery to do anything, you'd ruin the grain. So there you were.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, they don't have a problem now. How did they.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I didn't know now. You see, I've lost all track of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Could it be the quality of seed, or could it be farming methods, or could it be herbicides, or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, herbicides could they use it on the grain that's so close to those things, do you know?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Yeah, since it's not a grass. There are herbicides that would take out everything but the grass.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, well then, it's herbicides that's done it I guess. I didn't know how that was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the quality of the seed that the farmers are using now? Or would that have been mixed in with seed because it was growing in with wheat before, would it keep replicating?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it ought to clean out of wheat. It's smaller than wheat, but it isn't any shorter. It might be. Yeah, I think it'd clean out of wheat pretty well. Because they're different.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. We're starring to digress a little here. Okay, we're on page 23 and 24.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Did I fmish this? I guess so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This is about the most thorough, and kind of a long slow process doing it this way, but I think we're going to end up with a really excellent result.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I hope so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think we've got a good start and this is gonna.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let's see. Question, "Are you familiar with any of the plants maybe that the Indians used for food." "You bet." [Laughter] Quite sure of myself, wasn't I?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you were younger then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Well, you see my botany group has been playing with these Indian food plants. We've had contact with them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who would you recommend as, f you had to point to individuals that know a lot about these plants as Indian food, who, what lypes of individuals would. . . ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that wouldn't be easy, because it all depends on . . . they had to make a special study of it you see, and I just don't know them well enough.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about books, what books do you think. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, there are some books that you can find some, quite a bit of that information in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And do you think most of the books are pretty accurate?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yes. Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Do you know anybody in the Corvallis area that specialized in Indian food plants?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not particularly.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But there are some. See, when my botany teacher was living, I could get my questions answered!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's why we're asking you, of course, too!

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't learn the answers to all of them! [Pause] Now what were we looking at when I said "that's bitterroot"?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think we were looking at some photographs of some plants you had.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Yeah, that's right, you had some pictures.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I found one in eastern Oregon. That I recognized. But I found quite a plenty of yampah. See there aren't so awfully many

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think that most of your corrections with some of these older people and with some of the plants we discussed. You were saying, you didn't understand why the, or you didn't think the Indians had very many good plants.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, you would have thought, really, that they would have seen some worth having, or using, and cultivated them themselves. They just didn't get very far along the trail of civilization at all, did they?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, they didn't have metal. Do you think that maybe by using fire, that that was a method of cultivation that we 're just not used to looking at?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I guess. That's right, it isn't. And some of the tribes, I suppose, didn't have good ground.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now those in the Willamette Valley, you mentioned off the tape, that they might have had access to animals. But the ones in the Willamette Valley, from what we know, did exist mostly on vegetation and they did have good ground.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they could have done something. But they weren't interested in being civilized.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, but they didn't have metal or domestic animals, or alcohol. So maybe they. . . it depends on what you are calling civilized.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, they had cainas, and oak, and blackberries and strawberries, and onions, can you think of other plants that they might have needed in addition to that or plants that they could have cultivated better?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it's just too bad that they didn't get contact with the South American Indians and get potatoes and corn. You see, what they had, it took an awful lot of it to make much bulk.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you think that f certain species of plants had been introduced in the Willamette Valley then they could have done better?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, or anybody kind of help them get started on raising some good stuff.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think a limitation could have been that they didn't have metal?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I presume that that has something to do with it, because it was awfully hard to work with a stick.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. Page 28 here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [Pause]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And you see the Indians had always done it this way, and I have great respect for their ancestors. They didn't want to change it so much. What's this? "Yeah, different stuff, and that was something that would come in and hadn't been here naturally. But I don't remember any particular one." Then I thought, "Oh, yes, Tansy ragwort [Senecio jacobaea]." It was a stinker! Oh, about this, oh what we talked about. That papa told the woman to tear it up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, oh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] That's right. Bachelor button.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. That's a bad one. And there was one other one that he thought he could fight it by digging it up. And that it wasn't so thick. And that was the old man in the ground [Marah oreganus], a wild gourd. And that storage root, it had a storage root you see, big as a wild muskmelon. And he'd dig them up. He kept them pretty well down. [Pause] And that's another thing that was a difference between my dad and some of the other farmers. They didn't bother with these things.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: As far as controlling the weeds.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's right. Of course he worked himself to death.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, you know that Rohner said that and Marc/cs said that too, they said the other farmers didn't take care of their land as good as dad. Of course, he never lived to see.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah! [Laughter]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And both of them said the exact same thing, that their father really knew how to take care of the land, and their father died young.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Urn hmm. My father didn't reach 70.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think they meant younger than that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: "More like 50 years as her [Vida R. Bullis] husband was living when they moved out there." [Reading from page 32] I was just out there the other day and she's got more dahlias than ever.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you like dahlias?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, as a landscape flower. But it's a nuisance. You have to dig it up every fall and store the roots and plant it again in the spring.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] I've got some in front of my house I haven 't dug up and this is the third year they've come up.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, you can be lucky on the weather, but you see sometimes it gets you.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Well they're next to the foundation of the house and it probably keeps them a little warmer than they would out there. She couldn 't do that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] It gets colder out there anyway.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Probably.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Page 34.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let's see. "There's a while there, when Oregon just raised wheat until it wore the ground out." "AU the farmers raised wheat?" And that affected my paternal grandparents movements. They got eaten out by grasshoppers in Kansas, and came out here in their older age, expecting to start over again. They never got started to start! They came out here when the ground was just plum depleted with wheat. After several years they just wheated it to death. And he tried three different rented farms and it all depleted. Then he went out to Clatsop County and found it covered with trees. He couldn't win for losing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, one thing I'm curious about, how far south did the wheat crops get grown in the Willamette Valley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, just all over.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they as far south as Eugene?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, [think so. Everywhere there's reasonably level land you know, not so good in the hills,

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Wonder f that why the farmers around here claim now that you can't grow much in a lot of these places. You hear that a lot. Particularly in terms of the grass seed industry. They say the only thing you can grow out there is grass. I wonder if it's because of past farming practices.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, if they haven't done anything to make the land richer, I expect as they may feel the effects of that wheating.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I was told by one of my professors that wheat was grown no further south than Crescent Valley. We were on your family 'sfarm, and he said "This is as far south as wheat was grown."

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't feature that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you don't think that's true.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I doubt it very much.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Good.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But I couldn't stake my life on it. Now, what you call him, Van Smith [a old friend of Bessie], you ought to talk to about that. Because his father and his grandfather farmed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] At Smith Loop, out south of town. Yep.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] That's right, he would know, wouldn't he. Everybody keeps telling me I should talk to him.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Well you should

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, you better do that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] And you better do it quick.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And he's interesting to talk to.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And I remember seeing vetch come in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When did vetch come in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was grown I think, but I was still home. I hadn't got married yet I don't think. Just around that time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How old were you when you got married?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Twenty. Twenty-four, I think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Which vetch was it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Common. Sativa.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Oh, okay. Vicia Sativa. When did hairy vetch [Vicia villosa] come in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it was later. I don't know how much later. And sativa seemed to be the best one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Page 37.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [Pause] All these farms that had been established at any time at, at least, practically all of them had an old orchard. Now you see that one out there is rubbing 200 years.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now this is /dnd of interesting. We've talked about virtually everything I wanted to talk about except special trees and orchards.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] That one out there, you mean the one on your papa 's place.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Papa's place, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, the walnut orchard, are we talking about that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, that was put in after 1914. Well, no, I think that's the one he planted and when it bore he found out it was the wrong variety because it nearly always got frosted.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh!

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And he had to graft it, and made it later, much later getting it going.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, you say all the old places had orchards?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Those were just.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Family orchard of fruit, pears and apples, and everything the family would use.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now the orchard that the. . . so that's different from the walnut orchard?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now the walnut orchard we 'ye been calling the Gragg walnut orchard. But the family orchard, would that be?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Where you turn the corner to the left, that's the orchard between the house and the road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Does that orchard have a name, or was that associated with the family?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was just our family orchard.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] It was there when you moved.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it was there you see. And it was an old orchard then, so I figure it's about 200 years old!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, the first person that moved there, only went there 150 years ago so. . . but it was an old orchard.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] But it would have been planted then, probably with the first people that moved in.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, give or take 50 years!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Yeah, you couldn't go to Freds and buy apples back then. Do you recall any of the varieties in that orchard there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. There was a lot of them that were not good at all. But there were some humdingers! There was winesaps, they're wonderful winter apples. And belflowers would come on a little earlier. They're a long, yellow apple. And, what were some more of those?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A 20 ounce?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Or a blue pied?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the pears? Was there bartletts?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, and winter nellus, and. . . oh, what was that other pear? I used to know it. Shucks. Well, I'll think of it, but it was a thick, chubby pear. And the winter nellus was longer. And they were good. And then the summer apples, of course, the best one was a gravenstein. And those little red june, solid color red. And it wasn't a big apple, but it was good. And very white meat.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Called red june? Do you remember what you used the red junes for?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they came rather early. Just to eat raw.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you make them into salads?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Salads?!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Never had apple salad, huh? Ok.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yee gods, you couldn't get those old timers to eat a salad! [Laughter]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] So when was the first salad you remember?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, after I was married, probably.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Never had salad until you were an adult?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not as a salad. But we had some raw stuff you see, fruit or lettuce. Sliced cabbage. what do you call that?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Slaw?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we made kraut. Yes, slaw, that would be our main salad. Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] What did you do with lettuce?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. I don't remember cutting it up. I don't think we used it very much. I have an idea the slaw was better for us. I'm sure it had vitamin C in it. What was I trying to think of

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ttying to think of the name of an old thick-skinned pear? That was real good?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Or thick, not long and thin, but round. Oh, okay. Okay. Thick shaped pear.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. What was the name of it? Oh, shoot.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh well.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Go on to the next thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. We're on.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have noticed that the older people they were not brought up on salads as you are today. And they didn't want to eat it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Page 39 there. Another thing that's coming out of this. We 'ye got Cecil Compton. We've got 75 old pear and apple trees on 8 different orchards on school properties, and he 's telling use what the varieties are. We're trying to preserve these old orchards.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Good. Have ever met old Mr.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Smith.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Morris X?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes! Boy, he knows the varieties. And there's some, there's another old man, I can't think of now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, page 40.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [Pause] Papa didn't have time to hunt. But he did some. He didn't have time to go on rugged trips and deer hunt. If a deer come along and got in his way, why he might shoot it. But he did hunt pheasants. Cause they were so thick. And he didn't do it particularly for pleasure. He was too busy.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Well did you have problems with deer getting into stuff around the house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. I think one reason is dogs. We always had dogs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever see very many deer?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not many.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about beaver?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, none at all. The little streams out there are too little. [Pause] What's this' [Laughs] I sure explained why those people brought those foxes in!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You've got it covered.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: [Pause] Yeah, another silly thing to allow. Bringing the dang possums.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's see, that's 41? Page 42.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yep, my kid brother and I had fun catching little trout. Nine was a big one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Nine inches?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nine inches.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Guarantee two things, this is one of the best histories that we've got with the school, and it has caused us to go out and talk with a lot of other people, but I think it's gonna be one of the most thorough, too.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I hope so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, I think so.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Papa wasn't averse to hunting, but he hated to take so much time. From his work. So when they became a nuisance in the orchard, he just had to shoot them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they, in those days would they say that he was a "meat hunter," rather than a "sport hunter," or are you familiar with those terms?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, he was a. . . well how did they say that? Oh dear, that isn't right. Food on the table or something of the sort.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I think I know the phrase you are looking for. He hunted basically for the family table.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah!!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And when they come near, and got right in your way like roosting in the orchard, why he couldn't help himself. Let's see, "They were dairy farms?" "No, they were general farmers, and also good managers." [Bottom of page 43]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're on 44.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We're just going to town, aren't we?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, the last 15 or 20 pages, you have mostly "Yeah" and "Yes ", but you have a few comments.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Boy, this is a bad one. You know, they had a little bit of everything at one time or another, and a good farmer will have many. . . let's see, what's that. . . many irons in the fire, that's another expression. And if you just have one or two things that you've got to specialize in it very much to get anywhere fmancially. And he didn't miss any tricks having some of this and some of that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, they say things like "You don't put all your eggs in one basket ", or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, uh huh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Or would they just practice that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Practice, what do you mean?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Or would they actually have expressions saying to diversify, to have a lot of different crops, and expressions like "Don't put all your eggs in one basket" or would they just, you could tell by the way that they lived that they practiced those things. Or would they actually have phrases that they kind of followed or expressed their beliefs like that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I don't know too much about that. [Pause] Yeah, that cherry orchard was a little cash crop, but it give us kids, we kids a chance to make a little penny money, too, because people there weren't many orchards and people came and got them. And they would hire us to pick them sometimes, or they would, as I said before, they would ask us to pick them ourselves and ship them on the train to the. . . and they come to the . . . oh, now what am I trying to say? Where the. . . isn't that maddening?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Sort of like fruit stands, or something like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. Stations! Train stations! And get their boxes of cherries. We'd ship them that for. And boy we had to get up early that morning! We had to pick them, and we had to go in there with a horse, rig -- slow business -- and put them on the train.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where would they ship them to by train?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: To whatever station they wanted! Nearly always out toward the coast, like Kings Valley, and what are some of those? Chitwood, and various stations along there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] So, would a store owner come through then and buy them from you and have you ship them, or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no! Private citizens!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Oh really?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, we'd get a letter in the mail.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So somebody, li/ce, say at Nortons. Or one of those places, Marvel. They 'd say, send us a case of cherries, and away you'd go.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's interesting

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But we had to pick them. We had to get up early to do that. We had . . . the transportation you see was so slow, to get them into the station in time to go. They're a perishable crop, you see. And we couldn't do it one day and send them the next, we had to do it all in one day.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's interesting. They'd go by horse and buggy to train to right to somebody's doorstep!

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, not exactly.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Or to the station, yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Because they had to come to the train station.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] How would they find out that you had cherries?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. Well I suppose.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Word of mouth.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I suppose some of the older citizens that knew that, you see, right along, I don't know for certain. [Pause] Now what was this about the Indians? I guess this is the question, "Would there be pickers, like would Siletz Indians come across to pick or kids pick?" "Not Indians, but me and my brother."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, the Indians used to come out to the valley to pick hops.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Later on. Later on, for hops and not much else. That would be a pretty big deal. Then they'd come and camp, you see.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember any Indian camping places around town? Do you know why Squaw Creek is called Squaw Creek, going through.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No I don't know why. Where does it go?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: By the County fairgrounds.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. Hmm. No, there probably were several places, because we would dig up Indian relics.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's the last question I had for you here that we haven't covered yet. You talked about digging up Indian relics before. And you told me that it was on your family, your home.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, and I never thought about it, though, particularly, so I didn't mark the spot.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. So you're not exactly sure where on the family farm.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. But it's some place where it's plowed up or dug up or something, you see. So it was particularly deep.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would that be on the Graggfarin?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] And just sort of scattered all over the farm, or just in a particular place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, all over the valley, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] But there wasn't a particular concentration of them in one place, was there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There may have been, but I didn't know of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But it would be in an area that you plowed though, too. It wouldn 't be up like in the orchard, or it wouldn't be in oak woods. It'd be in areas where you plowed.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't think they would want to camp there. The trees are in the way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] But, now, I've found arrowheads where roads been bulldozed through. Just because the ground was turned up there, not because the Indians were there in any particular numbers. For a lot of farmers that I've talked to, and I've talked to the ones that were real interested in arrowheads, they can isolate a spot. The alfalfa field, and there are real concentrated spots. Edna Weise told me about a spot that's close to that camas prairie relict, and it's also real close to the Dixon Creek crossing on Applegate Trail, and that's a point of contact between the first people into the, the first Europeans, Euroamericans, and the Indian village. That's where disease got hit. Arrowheads and camas. It's all, they all started in that time.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Let's see now. "Because there are marks on some of them . . ." Oh yes, marks on some of them Well, see, he was very religious.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, you didn't want it in here?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Do you want it recorded or not?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it's part of the beliefs of the times.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'm real interested in that. We've been talking about the 2 by 2's and the different religious things, with some of the other.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Go ahead.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, anyway, she had one child born tongue tied, you know what that is? His tongue underneath the end was grown to his mouth. And he couldn't talk. And because he was born that way, she said the Lord made it, and she wouldn't change it. And that child had to grow up and earn the money to get it fixed. And he was pretty mad at his folks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall what kind of religion she had that taught her that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it was just ordinary Christian religion, I don't know what church. It wasn't any crazy, what do you call it? Well, not any different. But some people do crazy things.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you recall any of the religions coming through, or any tent meetings, or any unusual religious groups in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there was the holy rollers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Around here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In Corvallis

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever go to any of their meetings?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, you bet. [Laughter]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you become a holy roller?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why did you go to the meeting?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I thought you said, "Oh, you bet!" Did you hear any stories about what went on at the meetings?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I've heard something about the principles of the holy rollers. I don't think much of it. I didn't waste much time on it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On any religion or just that religion?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I went to the Christian church. That's what my mother belonged to. I didn't understand it and I don't think most others do.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We can turn this off if you want, but would you consider yourself a Christian?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you see a difference between Christianity and religion?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, there is a difference. Well, anybody's religion is religion, but it isn't all Christianity.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: So I consider myself a Christian. So anyway . . . now, what was I going to tell about? Oh, now you see we didn't know, keep up with Aunt Troth's family very well. She's the one that came with an ox team, wagons and ox team, in 1864. And settled down by Amity And she was lots . . . she was the oldest one in the family She was quite a bit older than my father. And her kids were all grown and married and moved, and we didn't move to where we were close enough to visit much. And anyway, about this boy, when he got old enough that he could get away from home and earned enough money so he could get his mouth fixed he did it. And now, my nephew is taking over the genealogy of the family And before he got so busy, they bought them this house so he could move in. They did quite a bit of work on it. And he found this fellow that had fixed . . . He was 84 years old then, I expect he's dead now. That was several years ago. And he went and hunted him up, he was up in Washington.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there's an interview with this uncle, then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that's with your nephew.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What's his name, so, your nephew's name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Same as my dad. Gragg. Lee Gragg. He lived with mamma. And I think that was fairly common, in those days. I don't know how it is yet. That what is, is and the Lord made it. And they don't do much about it. Nowadays, most anybody would have that simple operation and make life easier for anybody. And I think it's idiotic not to do it. Well, so, so it goes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Want to go to page 49 and call it a day?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I noticed how one thing leads to another. Somewhere here I told you about the going to the Lewis and Clark Exposition in 1905. And meeting up with Ezra Meeker. Now do either one of you know about Ezra Meeker?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Urn hrnm.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I saw the old fellow and his oxen.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You did?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And there's another thing that was a custom of the times. People drew away from, now how would I say that? Well anyway, they didn't like to be pushed into this and that and the other thing there. Some very good worthwhile things, it took a lot of pushing and prodding to get them to do it. And they objected to even marking the Oregon Trail.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There was objections to marking the Oregon Trail?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It couldn't get interest too much, for a long time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they against it, or just.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, against it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] What, just against change?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I guess so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they thought what Ezra Meeker was doing was not only boring, but it was wrong?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know if they thought it was wrong or not, but they didn't, didn't get hep with it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did you think?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I thought it was a fine thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there people that saw Ezra Meeker as kind of a hero?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, he became a hero later, too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Let's see, how old were you then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was about, in 1905 I was about 11.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] I'm right. Can you remember the forestry building?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What about that building sticks in your memory?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it was talked about much, and pointed out that there was lots of big timbers in there from our forest, you know. Made a fuss about it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it a big highlight?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, yeah. Let's see, what's this question here? "He kept it and rented it, and his children inherited it whole, and eventually I inherited some. Not much in those days as there was no shortage of land to buy then." Let's see. Might be I'm talking about Grandpa Crees? Yeah. He came in '71. And I read in the paper somewhere, not too long ago, that 1872 was the end of the period that you could be considered a pioneer.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. If you come later you're not. So he was a pioneer, but he's only just under the line.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] The last of the pioneers.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. [Laughter]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, now you can say you've got pioneer ancestry for sure then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, and the other grandpa didn't come to Oregon till '74, 50 he isn't. But this Aunt Trom did.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ah. Early pioneer.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now, it's funny. What did I do with that? Oh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] The pictures.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now that you've heard about Aunt Troth, maybe you. . . now this was Aunt Lessi's book. And I haven't read any of this Here's Aunt Lessi.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [PHIL] Oh, okay. I think I understand now, it's a fairly fancy book. More her style.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And this is the old family album, everybody had. Well here, that's Aunt Troth.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The one on the left?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you said the one on the right was.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Aunt Susan?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Your favorite.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You betcha.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was so nice about Aunt Susan?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, her disposition. She was kindness personified. And she never married, you see the both of them, it ran in their family, they had poor eyes. And she couldn't go to school extensively at all. And couldn't really . . . well of course in those days, women stayed home. But she had, when she could she would go and do housework, or home nursing, or anything she could do, you see, without an education. And her late years she lived with that the family. And I could look back and see where I could have done more for her, and it makes me mad I didn't. And that's what you can see, looking back.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This is your.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now this is grandpa.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, Gragg.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And his brother and two sisters, and the old devil.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I thought you said she was the grandmother of the devil?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, was the devil herself! [Laughter]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this is two brothers and two sisters and the other one.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's what I understand. And the generation I hadn't seen any of them but grandpa. They came from Pennsylvania.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so he was married the third time before he even came out here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, he caine out here and then when his second wife died, about two years later he farmed his children out with his friends and neighbors and went back and married her. And that's something else funny, that hitches up with a custom of the times. He farmed that Lessi out with Hamen Lewis. Hamen Lewis, it's not Hayman, it's Hamen.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Hamen? Good. Because I've got it as Herman, too.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Hamen. And she came home with body lice. That was not very common in those times!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Body lice?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Lice!! Yes!! Horrible. Now that is looked down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They was looking down on it in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Now it wouldn't be as horrified to get them. And I think this is one of grandpa's sisters, but I don't know for sure. Those are cousins, I don't know what degree of cousins.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now who, now this,.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And this is little Arthur Hall. Who was raised like a girl.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How old was he raised like a girl, till?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I don't think much longer. Because five years was about the limit.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, about five or six, and then they 'd.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, before they went to school they

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was a local family, wasn 't it, the Halls? Down in Corvallis, didn't you say?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. They had the bakery at that time. I don't know who this guy is. That's Mary Francis somebody, a cousin. I've heard of her. See, I acquired this in late life. And that's the little dress I showed you. Well anyway, .

entries.text: Bessie Gragg Murphy

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Bessie Gragg Murphy, 96, died at Corvallis Manor of natural causes Saturday.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: She was born in Elsie, Ore., to Stephen Alexander and Kate Crees Gragg. She moved with her family in 1900 to the Crescent Valley area near Corvallis, where she grew up on a farm.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: She graduated from Oregon Agricultural College in 1922 with a bachelor of science degree in home economics.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: On Aug. 6, 1922, she married Phillip G. Fleischman. He died in 1941.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: In 1952 she married Harry Murphy in Portland; he preceded her death.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Mrs. Murphy discovered an unnamed clover in 1962, which was named "Trifolium owyheense" by the botany department at Oregon State University.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: She was a member of the Pythian Sisters, Camp Fire Girls Leaders and the Corvallis Button Club, and was a volunteer on the election board of the Benton County Historical Society.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Mrs. Murphy enjoyed horse-back riding, botany, camping, genealogy, local history, button collecting and needlecraft. She was a member of the Handweavers and Spinners Guild.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Survivors include two daughters, Marjory Fitzwater of Lebanon and Phyllis Dentel of Oakridge; four grandchildren; eight great-grandchildren; and one nephew.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: She was preceded in death by one brother, George Gragg.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Visitation will be today from 1 to 5 p.m., Wednesday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and Thursday from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. at McHenry Funeral Home, 206 N.W. Fifth St., Corvallis.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Graveside services will be Thursday at 2 p.m. at Crystal Lake Cemetery in Corvallis. Memorial services will follow at 4:30 p.m. at the Benton County Historical Museum in Philomath.

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Donations in her memory may be made to the Benton County Historical Society and Museum in care of McHenry Funeral Home.
